body:
Kapil Sibal’s latest press conference with CJP leaders, pledging ₹1 crore and establishing a nationwide legal aid network for so-called “unjustly targeted” protesters, represents a deeply concerning pattern of selective advocacy that undermines the rule of law in India.

While the right to peaceful protest is fundamental, this initiative appears designed not to protect genuine victims of injustice but to shield those who disrupt public order, spread misinformation, and challenge the democratic mandate of the elected government under the guise of victimhood. 

Senior advocates and public figures like Mr. Sibal have a responsibility to strengthen institutions, not create parallel support systems that encourage frivolous litigation and embolden elements intent on destabilising national progress.

True justice demands accountability for violence, property damage, and attempts to derail critical examinations like NEET that affect millions of aspirants.

By framing legitimate law enforcement actions as persecution, this effort risks eroding public trust in our judiciary and police forces.

India deserves legal professionals who defend the Constitution impartially, not those who consistently align with narratives that weaken the nation’s resolve against internal disruptions.

The people are watching, and such partisan interventions will not go unchallenged in the court of public opinion.

body:
Both India and Italy are being hit by the same playbook right now, violent targeting of Modi, Meloni, and their law enforcement under the cover of “protests.”

In Italy, masked agitators stormed high-speed rail construction sites in Val di Susa. Stones, firecrackers, Molotovs, homemade devices. Over 120 police were hit and injured. Vehicles set ablaze. Organised, premeditated, and far from any spontaneous citizen gathering. Meloni herself called it out as organised violence.

In Delhi, the numbers are almost identical: 118+ police personnel hurt, including senior officers (Special CP, Joint CP, ACPs), during clashes with CJP demonstrators.

Two police buses attacked, shops on Janpath vandalised, stone-pelting, property damage. Police have flagged anti-social elements with criminal records mixing into the crowds via facial recognition. This is definiteluly not a pure “student protest.”

NEET was already reconducted with stricter measures after the paper-leak mess. Stringent action was taken. Yet it was kept alive as a ready-made weapon, exactly the kind of grievance that gets amplified, prolonged, and then turned into street confrontation when the timing suits. We all saw the attacks on police. Uniforms do not make the injuries any less real.

Notice the pattern: simultaneous pressure on the forces that maintain order in two countries whose leaders (Modi and Meloni) have built unusually close personal and strategic ties, Indo-Mediterranean partnership, defence-tech cooperation, open alignment against the usual globalist currents. 

When leaders who refuse the script get stronger, the forces of disruption target the thin blue line that stands between chaos and governance.

This DS has inserted the professional riot cadre, attack the police, flood the narrative with “peaceful students/protesters,” and force governments onto the defensive. Italy’s black-bloc style assault and Delhi’s stone-and-vandalism phase are not coincidence. They are the same method applied on two fronts.

The public should see the method for what it is.

body:
A viral video showing a man in Muslim attire attempting to throw a burning matchstick into the fuel tank of a damaged Mahindra Thar has been falsely shared on social media as footage from the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi, according to an Fact Check investigation.

The video, circulated after the July 20 Parliament march, was shared with claims that it showed a CJP supporter trying to set a vehicle on fire during the protest.

However, Fact Check found that the claim is false. The incident actually took place in Gaya, Bihar, and was unrelated to the NEET protest or the CJP demonstrations.

Using reverse image search, the fact-check team traced the same video to Instagram posts published by CNN-News18 and Moneycontrol on July 18, where it was identified as an incident that occurred following a road accident in Bihar.

According to a Dainik Bhaskar report cited by India Today, a Mahindra Thar collided with a motorcycle and an auto-rickshaw in Gaya, leaving two motorcyclists seriously injured.

Eyewitnesses reportedly claimed that the vehicle bore a BJP sticker and that a woman was driving it, although police did not officially confirm either allegation.

City SDPO Saroj Kumar only confirmed that two persons were injured in the accident and were undergoing treatment.

India Today's local stringer further confirmed that the incident occurred near the Gaya Civil Lines Police Station on July 16.

After the accident, a crowd gathered and some anti-social elements allegedly began pelting stones before attempting to set the vehicle ablaze.

Police later brought the situation under control and registered cases against both the owner and driver of the vehicle, as well as those accused of trying to burn it.

The misleading claim was also amplified by Republic Kannada news anchor Ranjith Shiriyara, who shared the same video multiple times on his social media accounts.

The posts presented the Bihar incident as being connected to the CJP-led NEET protest, despite the video later being fact-checked as unrelated to the Delhi demonstrations.

Meanwhile, the fact-check has gained significance after BJP MLC C.T. Ravi, who recently came under fire for his remarks about "mullahs" during a BJP protest over the NEET controversy in Chikkamagaluru, claimed at a press conference that his comments were made in reference to this viral video.

Ravi had earlier remarked, "What does a mullah have to do with the NEET examination? Even if you tear open his chest, you won't find three letters written there," drawing criticism.

Following a complaint alleging that the speech promoted communal hatred, Chikkamagaluru Town Police registered an FIR against him under provisions relating to promoting enmity and hate speech.

After the FIR was registered, Ravi told reporters that he was referring to the viral video showing a Muslim man trying to set a vehicle on fire and had questioned why such a person would be associated with the NEET protests.

However, the Fact Check establishes that the video Ravi referred to was not from the Delhi protest and had no connection with the CJP agitation.

Instead, it depicted an unrelated incident of mob violence following a traffic accident in Gaya, Bihar. The claim linking the video to the NEET protests was false.

The misleading claim was also amplified by Republic Kannada news anchor Ranjith Shiriyara, who shared the same video multiple times on his social media accounts.

The posts presented the Bihar incident as being connected to the CJP-led NEET protest, despite the video later being fact-checked as unrelated to the Delhi demonstrations.
#FactCheck

body:
Nine years ago, S Anitha became the first victim of NEET in Tamil Nadu, and one of the most prominent faces of Tamil Nadu’s fight against NEET.

In 2017, the 17-year-old from Ariyalur had scored 1,176 out of 1,200 marks in her Class 12 Tamil Nadu State Board exams. Her medical cut-off score was 196.75 out of 200 — marks that would have placed her among medical aspirants under Tamil Nadu’s earlier admission system.

But that year, NEET became mandatory for medical admissions. Anitha, who had prepared through the state-board syllabus, could not secure a medical seat through the national entrance exam. She became one of the earliest voices opposing NEET in Tamil Nadu, arguing that a common entrance test would disadvantage students from rural areas, government schools and marginalised communities.

Anitha’s brother S. Manirathnam, who has now joined the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi, says her fight was deeply personal.

He says Anitha was raised by their father, a daily wage labourer, after their mother died when she was seven. He recalls that Anitha wanted to become a doctor because their mother’s death due to an illness had shaped her dream of entering medicine.

“She wanted to become a doctor because she had seen the suffering caused by the lack of medical care,” Manirathnam said, recalling his sister’s journey.

Anitha joined the legal battle against NEET and became one of the petitioners before the Supreme Court, seeking relief for Tamil Nadu students. The Court did not grant the exemption sought by the state, and days later, on 1 September 2017, Anitha died by suicide at her home in Ariyalur.

Speaking about the impact of NEET on his family, Manirathnam said, “NEET has destroyed my family.”

Years later, he has joined the CJP protest, saying Tamil Nadu’s opposition to NEET began with students like Anitha, who questioned whether a single national entrance exam could account for the inequalities faced by students across the country.

🚨STATEMENT

We are deeply concerned by multiple reports reaching us of students and other protestors being targeted, detained, or arrested by various state agencies, particularly in Assam, West Bengal, and Bihar.

The Cockroach Janta Party had called off its nationwide protest only after the Government of India assured us that no punitive action would be taken against any protestor, either now or in the future, in any BJP-ruled or NDA-ruled states. The reports emerging from these states are therefore a matter of grave concern.

First, we wish to assure every protestor that our legal team is already coordinating with brilliant lawyers in the concerned states to secure the release of those detained and to extend all possible legal assistance. This has been happening from Day 1.

Second, we call upon the Government of India, particularly @JPNadda ji and @DrJitendraSingh ji, to immediately honour the assurance given to us by ensuring the release of those detained and by directing that no coercive or retaliatory action is taken against any protestor anywhere in the country. The FIRs registered ought to be withdrawn too.

The Government of India is also reminded of its commitment to furnish us the written guarantee in this regard by tomorrow, Tuesday, 28 July 2026.

Our decision to suspend the nationwide protest was taken in good faith and solely on the basis of the government’s assurance that it would stand by its word. Any departure from that assurance would not merely amount to a breach of trust with the Cockroach Janta Party but would also be a breach of public trust with lakhs of young Indians who chose dialogue over protests.

Such breach of trust will be completely unacceptable to the youth.

The Government of India is reminded that it derives credibility not from just making a promise, but from the promises they honour.

To the young protestors we say, hold on. We are with you. The CJP continues to closely monitor the situation and expects the Government of India and all BJP/NDA state governments to act with utmost urgency, responsibility, and good faith that the present circumstances demand. We demand that all detainees/arrestees be released immediately, and in any case by tomorrow, and that all FIRs be withdrawn immediately, failing which we shall take further necessary steps.

TG Mohandas, a former head of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) Intellectual Cell and a political commentator associated with the Rashtiya Swayansevak Sangh (RSS) in Kerala, said the protesters at Jantar Mantar would have been shot and killed if he was in control. He also said the women who were part of the protest like to be raped and would not even complaint if it happens.

The derogatory comments against students and other citizens who participated in the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest, demanding accountability in the NEET paper leak, in Delhi were made through multiple videos published on a YouTube channel called Pathrika.

In a video published on July 26, he explained how he would handle the situation, if he was in charge. “I will impose a curfew in that area. I will announce the crowd to disperse three times. Then I will shoot, people will scatter and run. Some may die and some may suffer injuries. Within four hours the situation will be calm. The bodies will be collected and taken to hospitals,” he said.

In another video, he said that if the police withdrew from the protest site, rapes would happen.

“Rapes will happen, mass rapes…there are girls who like rape…there are people who like rapes, especially, leftist, secular, democratic, proletarian class of people…if someone dies because of this, they will get a martyr…When mass rapes happen there won't be any complaints, because these are the people who like rape,” Mohandas says in the video.

The videos were published after the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan following a 36-day protest by the CJP.

In another video published on July 24, Mohandas is seen encouraging physical assault on student protesters. He stated that police have every right to hide their name badges and claimed that students were appearing in police uniforms at Jantar Mantar. “Police beat them inside the barricade and outside the barricade; the police were also beaten up,” he said.

Mohandas is a commentator who has a significant following in Kerala. Many have demanded his arrest over the comments.

body:
56 inch Chest with a 26 inch Spine

BJP surrendered to the Cockroach Janata Party. Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. All FIRs against protesters withdrawn. Compensation for NEET victims accepted. Every single demand met. The 37-day protest at Jantar Mantar ended with CJP posting "Cockroaches won. Democracy won."

This did not have to end this way. And one of the main reasons it did is sycophancy.

For those of us who have been following Indian politics long enough, this movie is familiar. We watched it play out with the Congress party over two decades. The script is the same. Only the cast has changed.

Here is how the sycophancy spiral works.

A powerful leader consolidates authority. The people closest to them rise not because of their ability but because of their loyalty. These loyalists tell the leader what the leader wants to hear. Criticism is treated as disloyalty. Disagreement is treated as betrayal. Over time, the leader becomes surrounded by people whose only skill is praise. JP Nadda. Gogoi. Sanjay Jha. Digvijay Singh. Different parties, same species. They thrive not by being strong but by making the leader feel strong.

The problem is not that these people are sycophants. The problem is what sycophancy does to the information flow.

BJP's own supporters have been demanding Pradhan's resignation for months over the NEET examination scandal. Students died by suicide. Parents were devastated. The anger was real, widespread, and legitimate. But the people around Modi told him it was a non-issue. That the noise would die down. That the party's core support would hold. That Pradhan need not resign because resigning would show weakness.

This is what sycophants do. They filter reality. They present the world as the leader wants to see it, not as it is. And the leader, addicted to the dopamine of constant positive feedback, treats any dissonance as noise rather than signal. When you are in a sycophantic spiral, you are so accustomed to praise that even mild criticism feels like an attack. So you default to more praise. More reassurance. More "everything is fine, sir."

Until it is not fine. Until a satirical movement born from a Chief Justice's insult to unemployed youth puts people on the street and forces your Health Minister to sit across from two 20-somethings and accept every demand they put on the table.

Watch the footage of Nadda meeting the CJP representatives. This is India's Health Minister, a senior BJP leader, practically begging for a handshake. This is what sycophancy produces. Not strength. Weakness dressed in a party robes. When the moment demanded firmness, strategic communication, and a genuine engagement with legitimate grievances, the party sent a man whose instinct was to surrender because he had never been trained to fight. He was trained to agree.

Nadda showed BJP's core voters that the 56-inch chest has deputies with 26-inch spines.

This is the real cost. Elections are not won by core voters alone. Core voters will vote BJP no matter what. But elections are won by swing voters. And swing voters are watching. They are watching Nadda fumble. They are watching the party that projects strength act from weakness. They are watching a satirical Instagram movement outmaneuver the most formidable political machine in Indian history.

Even if swing voters are lost, core voters can be demoralized. They may never switch loyalties. But they may not show up at the polling booth. The dissonance for them is real. They signed up for a party that fights. A party that does not bend. When they see their leaders bend on national television, the gap between the party's self-image and its behavior becomes too wide to ignore. They may not articulate it. But the enthusiasm fades. The booth-level energy drops. The margins shrink.

Congress walked this exact path. A formidable force reduced to losing official opposition status within a decade. Not because the public turned against them overnight. But because the sycophants drowned out the grassroots leaders. Because the Digvijay Singhs, Gogois, Mani Shankars and Sanjay Jhas rose while the genuine talent was sidelined. Because the leadership stopped hearing the truth and started hearing only what made them comfortable.

BJP has one structural advantage Congress never had: it is not wedded to a dynasty. It has the RSS's organizational depth. It has a self-correction mechanism. But sycophancy corrodes self-correction. When the leadership structure is infested with weak men who have no real connect or command, the mechanism rusts.

Modi and Shah can clean house. They can replace the Naddas with fighters. They can rebuild the feedback loops that once made BJP the most responsive political organization in the country. But that requires acknowledging that the problem exists. And acknowledging that the problem exists requires hearing it from someone other than a sycophant.

That is the trap. And it is the same trap Congress walked into. And in all likelihood, BJP will continue to walk into.

Before BJP IT Cell floods your feed with...
"Modi Masterstroke."
Let's call it what it looks like.
A "Stupidstroke."

Dharmendra Pradhan had to go.
No debate.

India's education system is rotten.
It needed surgery.

Not slogans.
Not committees.
Not another press conference.

A complete overhaul.

But timing is everything.

The government did not remove him after reform.
It removed him after pressure.

And that changes everything.

CJP had no proven national student base.
No moral legitimacy to dictate terms to the Government.

Yet this government served legitimacy to it...
On a silver platter.

Now they can proudly say:
"We forced a Union Minister to resign."

Congratulations!!!

You have just manufactured a political brand.

Tomorrow...
A political party.
A pressure cartel.
An unelected veto machine.

A B-team of AAP that quietly slices BJP's own vote bank.

BJP has seen this movie before.

It surrendered the Farm Laws.
Now it has surrendered a Minister.

Not because accountability was wrong.

But because the street learnt something far more dangerous.

Pressure works.
Or worse...
Violence works.

That is the real headline.

Once a protest tastes blood...
It doesn't ask for dessert.
It asks for the kitchen.

Today...
Dharmendra Pradhan.

Tomorrow...
Action against the police.

Then another Minister.
Then the Home Minister.

Eventually...
Narendra Modi.

What a Masterstroke.

Bravo.

You didn't end the protest.
You upgraded its business model.

When governments reward pressure...
Pressure becomes policy.

When governments reward street muscle...
Street muscle becomes strategy.

And when survival becomes more important than reform...
Reform is the first casualty.

The tragedy is this.

Nobody will now discuss NEET reforms.
Nobody will discuss NTA reforms.
Nobody will discuss paper leaks.
Nobody will discuss fixing the system.

The system disappears.
The spectacle survives.

CJP has not ended.
It has just learnt one lesson.

The Government can be made to kneel.

He is Vibhu Gautam.

He made abusive remarks against the Indian Army during the CJP protest.

After his video went viral, some people decided that he should be handed over to the police. However, when they went to his house, they found out that his father is disabled. Seeing his father's situation, they decided not to pursue getting him arrested. Instead, they asked him to apologize, and he later recorded and posted a video apologizing.

Is it wrong to protest against the NEET paper leak or to demand the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan? No, not at all.

But that is not what he did. Instead, he came to the protest and started making abusive remarks against the Indian Army. He is not a child who cannot distinguish between right and wrong. He is old enough to understand the remarks he is making and the legal consequences of his actions.

His mindset led him to believe that it was the moment to turn India into another Nepal or Bangladesh. Many people like him also fail to understand that when they move away from the actual cause of a protest and engage in propaganda and anti-India activities, they may face serious legal consequences. Their careers and futures could be affected. In his case, even his father had to apologize because of his son's actions.

This period of unrest is temporary. The protests will eventually end. Those with political ambitions will move on and continue with politics. But common people like us may end up facing the consequences.

In the end, all that remains is regret.
By the time you realize the cost of your actions, the damage is already done. It can leave behind years of legal trouble, a damaged reputation, lost opportunities, and a burden that lasts far longer than the protest itself.

body:
Dear @narendramodi @PMOIndia @dpradhanbjp @JoshiPralhad 🙏

Just heard an interesting conversation near the lift lobby of my apartment.

A few girls were talking about the NEET protest. One of them said, "Look at the NEET protest by CJP. They got justice by forcing the Education Minister to resign." Another added, "The Education Minister doesn't even know how to write a resignation letter."

One of the girls recognised me and said, "Sorry, uncle. We didn't mean anything bad." Then she asked, "Uncle, what do you think?"

By then, the lift had arrived and we all got in.

I just told her, "Never believe the first piece of information you receive on any app. Verify it. Read more. Dig deeper. See who is saying it, what their background is, and what kind of language they themselves have used in public. After that, form your own opinion. The decision is yours."

My floor arrived, and I stepped out.

That conversation stayed with me.

We can criticise people we disagree with, and everyone has the right to question public figures. But what worries me more is how quickly misinformation and propaganda spread through social media. Many young people end up believing the first version of a story they see without checking if it is even true.

At that age, it is easy to believe that every movement is a revolution and that every resignation is the solution to a problem. Real life is much more complicated than that.

The bigger concern is that we are slowly losing our children to misinformation. They deserve facts, not manipulation.

So instead of ignoring them or shouting at them, let us talk to them. Encourage them to question, verify, and think for themselves.

That is our responsibility as parents, elders, teachers, and as a society.

18-year-old NEET aspirant Sharim allegedly died by suicide on 13 June following the alleged NEET-UG paper leak controversy. A resident of Amarpur village in Uttar Pradesh's Bulandshahr district, Sharim had been preparing for NEET at Aakash Institute in Jasola, Delhi.

His elder brother, Firoz Qureshi, says he has been seeking justice ever since. According to Firoz, he first approached the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), requesting that Sharim's photograph and details be displayed on the protest stage, but alleges that his request was ignored.

Firoz further claims that on 15 June, he went to Shaheen Bagh Police Station to file a complaint, but alleges that the police did not take his concerns seriously.

According to Firoz, he made one final attempt on the last morning of the Jantar Mantar protest to raise his brother's case with CJP representatives, but says he was once again ignored.

Dear @narendramodi @PMOIndia @dpradhanbjp @JoshiPralhad 🙏

Just heard an interesting conversation near the lift lobby of my apartment.

A few girls were talking about the NEET protest. One of them said, "Look at the NEET protest by CJP. They got justice by forcing the Education Minister to resign." Another added, "The Education Minister doesn't even know how to write a resignation letter."

One of the girls recognised me and said, "Sorry, uncle. We didn't mean anything bad." Then she asked, "Uncle, what do you think?"

By then, the lift had arrived and we all got in.

I just told her, "Never believe the first piece of information you receive on any app. Verify it. Read more. Dig deeper. See who is saying it, what their background is, and what kind of language they themselves have used in public. After that, form your own opinion. The decision is yours."

My floor arrived, and I stepped out.

That conversation stayed with me.

We can criticise people we disagree with, and everyone has the right to question public figures. But what worries me more is how quickly misinformation and propaganda spread through social media. Many young people end up believing the first version of a story they see without checking if it is even true.

At that age, it is easy to believe that every movement is a revolution and that every resignation is the solution to a problem. Real life is much more complicated than that.

The bigger concern is that we are slowly losing our children to misinformation. They deserve facts, not manipulation.

So instead of ignoring them or shouting at them, let us talk to them. Encourage them to question, verify, and think for themselves.

That is our responsibility as parents, elders, teachers, and as a society.

STORY | Anti paper leak bill with stricter punishment introduced in Lok Sabha

Government on Monday introduced a bill in the Lok Sabha to amend the anti-paper leaks law with stricter punishment of up to 10 years in jail and a Rs 50 lakh fine, within days of large-scale student protests against the NEET fiasco rocking the nation that forced Dharmendra Pradhan to resign as education minister.

The proposed legislation was introduced by Minister of State for PMO Jitendra Singh amidst protests and sloganeering by the Opposition demanding a response from the government over the police crackdown on students during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led July 20 protest march to Parliament.

According to the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, investigations into paper leak cases are to be completed within two months.

The bill says that individuals involved in paper leaks or unfair means in exams will get jail terms for a minimum of 5 years and a maximum of 10 years and a fine of up to Rs 50 lakh.

For organised crimes, the bill proposes a minimum sentence of seven years and a fine of up to Rs 10 crore.

TG Mohandas, a former head of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) Intellectual Cell and a political commentator associated with the Rashtiya Swayansevak Sangh (RSS) in Kerala, said the protesters at Jantar Mantar would have been shot and killed if he was in control. He also said the women who were part of the protest like to be raped and would not even complaint if it happens.

The derogatory comments against students and other citizens who participated in the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest, demanding accountability in the NEET paper leak, in Delhi were made through multiple videos published on a YouTube channel called Pathrika.

In a video published on July 26, he explained how he would handle the situation, if he was in charge. “I will impose a curfew in that area. I will announce the crowd to disperse three times. Then I will shoot, people will scatter and run. Some may die and some may suffer injuries. Within four hours the situation will be calm. The bodies will be collected and taken to hospitals,” he said.

In another video, he said that if the police withdrew from the protest site, rapes would happen.

“Rapes will happen, mass rapes…there are girls who like rape…there are people who like rapes, especially, leftist, secular, democratic, proletarian class of people…if someone dies because of this, they will get a martyr…When mass rapes happen there won't be any complaints, because these are the people who like rape,” Mohandas says in the video.

The videos were published after the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan following a 36-day protest by the CJP.

In another video published on July 24, Mohandas is seen encouraging physical assault on student protesters. He stated that police have every right to hide their name badges and claimed that students were appearing in police uniforms at Jantar Mantar. “Police beat them inside the barricade and outside the barricade; the police were also beaten up,” he said.

Mohandas is a commentator who has a significant following in Kerala. Many have demanded his arrest over the comments.

body:
A Conversation That Confirmed What I Was Already Thinking.

This morning, my phone rang. The caller is a hardcore NCP, Congress, and Shiv Sena (UBT) sympathiser who also holds an important organisational position in one of the MVA parties.

After the usual greetings, our conversation naturally shifted to the ongoing NEET protests—the aftermath, why they happened, and what they could mean for the BJP now.

Let me make one thing clear: he is an MVA sympathiser. Yet what he said echoed almost exactly what had been running through my own mind.

Last week, I had written that the BJP's political calculations had gone badly wrong in the NEET paper leak issue. The matter escalated to the point where the Prime Minister had to release three videos, a Union Minister resigned, and the government found itself on the defensive.

First, the BJP has historically been quick to recognise public sentiment and respond when the mood on the streets becomes impossible to ignore. That does not mean it will now bow to every protest. If anything, this episode should encourage the government to become more transparent, accountable, and proactive. Secondly, So those of you, expecting now protests will be the next big thing all the time, dream on!

The next issue brewing up is the ethanol controversy 

Tehseen Poonawalla has raised questions that deserve answers, and it increasingly appears that Nitin Gadkari could become the next political target. Unlike former Union Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, Gadkari has had a much longer public and political career, giving opponents far more material to scrutinise. Whether that translates into anything substantial remains to be seen.

Coming back to my conversation, the MVA sympathiser told me something I completely agreed with.

He said:

"Vikrant, even many people on the Right did not like what happened during these protests. Even many of the Right too supported the students and demanded transparency, but the abusive attacks on the Prime Minister, the assault on policemen, and the destruction of public property crossed the line."

I agreed.

The genuine students who sparked this movement should never become collateral damage. If peaceful students have faced punitive action, the government should review those cases and withdraw action wherever appropriate.

Interestingly, CJP founder Dipke himself acknowledged that anti-India elements and disruptive groups had infiltrated the protests to hijack a legitimate student movement.

What Exactly Is CJP's Objection?

Dipke had earlier stated that those responsible for violence, abusive slogans, and unlawful acts were outsiders who did not represent his supporters.

If that is indeed the case, then shouldn't CJP support action against those specific individuals instead of opposing the entire law enforcement process?

Those who attacked police personnel, vandalised public property, or attempted to derail a peaceful student movement should face the law. Innocent students, however, should be protected.

If CJP itself accepts that anti-social elements infiltrated the protests, then why is it now objecting to the government's action against those accused of violence?

That is a question that deserves an answer.

A New Lease of Life for the Opposition in Maharashtra? 

There is little doubt that this episode has injected fresh energy into an opposition that had appeared politically dormant, particularly in Maharashtra. Dipke has, for the moment, given it a rallying point.

However, Maharashtra is a politically unique state.

Many opposition parties may now attempt to replicate this strategy through younger leaders such as Aaditya Thackeray and Rohit Pawar. But there is one major difference.

People are still trying to understand who Dipke is. Leaders such as Aaditya Thackeray, Rohit Pawar, Uddhav Thackeray, and Raj Thackeray are already familiar political faces. Voters have watched them for years and have largely formed their opinions.

For that reason, I am not convinced that the same political formula will produce identical results in Maharashtra.

Even if much of Bollywood or other influential voices oppose the BJP, Maharashtra's politics has traditionally been shaped more by local political realities than celebrity endorsements.

Whether this momentum becomes a lasting political movement or remains a temporary surge of public anger is something only time will answer.

Vikrant Meena Hemant Joshi.

body:
A viral video showing a man in Muslim attire attempting to throw a burning matchstick into the fuel tank of a damaged Mahindra Thar has been falsely shared on social media as footage from the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi, according to an Fact Check investigation.

The video, circulated after the July 20 Parliament march, was shared with claims that it showed a CJP supporter trying to set a vehicle on fire during the protest.

However, Fact Check found that the claim is false. The incident actually took place in Gaya, Bihar, and was unrelated to the NEET protest or the CJP demonstrations.

Using reverse image search, the fact-check team traced the same video to Instagram posts published by CNN-News18 and Moneycontrol on July 18, where it was identified as an incident that occurred following a road accident in Bihar.

According to a Dainik Bhaskar report cited by India Today, a Mahindra Thar collided with a motorcycle and an auto-rickshaw in Gaya, leaving two motorcyclists seriously injured.

Eyewitnesses reportedly claimed that the vehicle bore a BJP sticker and that a woman was driving it, although police did not officially confirm either allegation.

City SDPO Saroj Kumar only confirmed that two persons were injured in the accident and were undergoing treatment.

India Today's local stringer further confirmed that the incident occurred near the Gaya Civil Lines Police Station on July 16.

After the accident, a crowd gathered and some anti-social elements allegedly began pelting stones before attempting to set the vehicle ablaze.

Police later brought the situation under control and registered cases against both the owner and driver of the vehicle, as well as those accused of trying to burn it.

The misleading claim was also amplified by Republic Kannada news anchor Ranjith Shiriyara, who shared the same video multiple times on his social media accounts.

The posts presented the Bihar incident as being connected to the CJP-led NEET protest, despite the video later being fact-checked as unrelated to the Delhi demonstrations.

Meanwhile, the fact-check has gained significance after BJP MLC C.T. Ravi, who recently came under fire for his remarks about "mullahs" during a BJP protest over the NEET controversy in Chikkamagaluru, claimed at a press conference that his comments were made in reference to this viral video.

Ravi had earlier remarked, "What does a mullah have to do with the NEET examination? Even if you tear open his chest, you won't find three letters written there," drawing criticism.

Following a complaint alleging that the speech promoted communal hatred, Chikkamagaluru Town Police registered an FIR against him under provisions relating to promoting enmity and hate speech.

After the FIR was registered, Ravi told reporters that he was referring to the viral video showing a Muslim man trying to set a vehicle on fire and had questioned why such a person would be associated with the NEET protests.

However, the Fact Check establishes that the video Ravi referred to was not from the Delhi protest and had no connection with the CJP agitation.

Instead, it depicted an unrelated incident of mob violence following a traffic accident in Gaya, Bihar. The claim linking the video to the NEET protests was false.

The misleading claim was also amplified by Republic Kannada news anchor Ranjith Shiriyara, who shared the same video multiple times on his social media accounts.

The posts presented the Bihar incident as being connected to the CJP-led NEET protest, despite the video later being fact-checked as unrelated to the Delhi demonstrations.

body:
🚩I was part of the protest march in Delhi, saw democratic politics take a new turn

(Sensible Article by  YOGENDRA YADAV,who says Parliament and much of Lutyens' Delhi was packed with the protesters. It was India's "Oc-cupy moment. Anger against Minister Dharmendra Pradhan is only the tip of the iceberg. The underlying urge is for an equitable, meaningful and quality education and for a universal right to employment.For many months now, I have been re-peating a dialogue to anyone who asks me about the future of India: "Sawal ye nahin hai kijanatatanashahi ke khilaaf kharihogi ya nahin. Sawal sirf itna hai ki jab janata kharihogitab tak kahin ham toh nahin baith jayenge". Yesterday, I saw it unfold before my eyes )

THE REGIME-and the silence - often made me wonder whether I'm completely crazy for coming back... But today  to see this democratic spirit which has been silenced for so long come back alive again - I feel whole again. Even if temporarily".

I read these lines well past 3 am, still trying to process all that I had witnessed on the streets of Delhi this Monday. These lines, posted on X by Vanya Vaidehi Bhargav, her-self a fine political theorist, captured why July 20 may be remembered in the history of Indian democracy.

This column has argued that as we slip from competitive authoritarianism to electoral autocracy, the focus of the Opposition must switch from electoral politics to a politics of resistance. Here are six reasons why the Jantar Mantar protest was a perfect illustration of what the politics of resistance may look like.

Firstly, the numbers. No one has a good estimate. But it was undoubtedly many times more than the 15,000-20,000 the or ganisers had hoped and planned for. Drone images suggest that well over a lakh joined this protest. Originally planned as a march, it turned into a rally, then a raila a mass flow. By the afternoon, every road leading to

Parliament and much of Lutyens' Delhi was packed with the protesters. It was India's "Oc-cupy moment.

What made the numbers stand out even more is that this was an organic mobilisation. Far from the culture of rent-a-crowd political rallies or spectacles of organisa-tional prowess, the Jantar Mantar protest comprised almost entirely self-mobilised youth responding to a social media call, ar-anging for their travel and walking long distances. The last time I witnessed this spontaneous synchronisation was the fa-mous Republic Day tractor march organ-ised by the farmers' movement in 2021.

Third, notice their "utterly absurd diversity", as a friend called it. I met a person who travelled from Arunachal Pradesh, a group of adults from Dharamshala in Himachal Pradesh, a wheel-chair bound student of Spanish, a group of girls from Dehradun, scores of boys and girls from all over UP, Bihar and MP, students from elite private universities, national public universities as well as time-pass colleges, and of course a large chunk of "aspirants" from Mukherjee Nagar and similar hotspots. The proportion of women was striking and exhilarating. These were not your usual suspects. An overwhelming majority were first-time par-ticipants in any protest. Their families mostly supported the BJP. So did they, till yesterday. That must worry the regime.

Fourth, the issue that brought them together was much larger and more enduring than just the recent paper leaks. There were, of course, students who suffered the NEET cancellation and the CBSE scam, parents who lost their children due to this fiasco, aspirants waiting indefinitely for jobs, and victims of recruitment scams. But more than direct sufferers, the protesters were primarily potential sufferers, those who know that it could be their turnto-morrow, those who realise that the educa-tion-employment system has broken down.

More than direct sufferers , the protesters were primarily potential sufferers, those who know that it could be their turn tomorrow, those who realise that the education-employment system has broken down

Anger against Minister Dharmendra Pradhan is only the tip of the iceberg. The underlying urge is for an equitable, meaningful and quality education and for a universal right to employment. It is after half a century-since the JP movement in Bihar in 1974-that a youth protest has placed education and employment at the centre of the national agenda.

Fifth, the spirit of resistance goes beyond names and labels. Sonam Wangchuk is clearly their hero, but the hero-worship quo-tient is much more muted than during the Anna movement. The youth related to the CJP and its leadership, but were not shy to offer healthy criticism. They heard and cheered political leaders and activists from the podium, but were not swayed by anyone personality. This democratic spirit augurs well for the future.

Sixth, the repeated chants of "Godi media, go back" were a reminder that the youth have found a way past the narratives of mainstream media. For the last one

month, the Noida channels and the notional press more or less erased the protest at Jantar Mantar, when not mocking or demonising it. Yet every calculation of the regime and every narrative of its spin doctors was defied. Just as in the farmers' movement, media black-outs ac tually spurred the participants into developing their parallel informa-tion channels through social media, word of mouth and Whats-

App. Their posters were punchy: "The true test of a democracy isn't the protest. It'show the state responds to it". Their slogans were innovative. I heard this one for the first time: "Jab jab Modi darta hai, Hindu-Muslim karta hai". The authoritarian narrative is being punctured.

Seventh, and above all, July 20 shows a fracturing of the spell of fear. Today's youth understand the risks of surveillance and pro-filing under the present regime, something absent during the Ramlila Maidan mobilisa-tion of the anti-corruption movement. That deterred many of them from coming to Jan-tar Mantar for the first two weeks. But somehow, something shattered it on Monday. Perhaps the safety of the crowd. Perhaps the adrenaline of hopelessness. Or maybe a faint hope. But these young people were not afraid of being heard, photo-graphed or even tear-gassed.

Finally, in a way almost unnoticed, the movement could mark a new phase in the politics of social justice. The youth of India have come together in a movement led by a Dalit, Abhijeet Dipke, and inspired by an Adi-vasi, Sonam Wangchuk, one not limited to the stereotypical "SC/ST issues". Instead of demanding its share in the nation, bahujan politics can now define what the nation is.

For many months now, I have been re-peating a dialogue to anyone who asks me about the future of India: "Sawal ye nahin hai kijanatatanashahi ke khilaaf kharihogi ya nahin. Sawal sirf itna hai ki jab janata kharihogitab tak kahin ham toh nahin baith jayenge". Yesterday, I saw it unfold before my eyes. 

The writer is member, Swaraj India, and national convenor, Bharat Jodo Abhiyaan. Views are personal

body:
🚩Modi govt can’t see the difference between confidence and arrogance. What it means to people ?

(It’s not just about the NEET paper leaks anymore. It’s not even about Dharmendra Pradhan. The huge gathering is a cumulative effect of small grievances that have been building up.When protesters talk about the government’s refusal to engage with the youth, they are only voicing their frustration with a system in which they have no say.)

In the 2016 film Sultan, Anushka Sharma’s character gives her wrestler-husband Sultan—played by Salman Khan—a stinging rebuke for ‘earning’ arrogance while she wanted him to earn respect: “Maine tujhe izzat kamaane ko kaha tha. Tu toh guroor kamaa ke aa gaya Sultan.” Many Indians may relate to her better now.

On Monday, the might of the State was on display as the police lathicharged and used tear gas to prevent thousands of young demonstrators from reaching the Parliament to protest against irregularities in medical entrance examinations and demand the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Activist Sonam Wangchuk, who was on fast for three weeks before being forcibly taken to Safdarjung Hospital, couldn’t join them as he said he was under ‘illegal detention’.

Even as thousands of students were struggling to cross police barricades to reach the Parliament, Prime Minister Narendra Modi delivered his customary address before the start of the session. He made no mention of what was happening to India’s youth barely a few hundred metres from where he stood. As if they didn’t matter! Lauding the successful launch of a rocket by a Hyderabad-based company, he took a not-so-veiled swipe at Rahul Gandhi, saying that the feat was achieved by those with an average age of 28 years, “not some 56-year-old young man”. It was out of context. The joke was supposed to be on the 56-year-old Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha. But its timing—with the State’s brute power on display against students and youth in the national capital—seemed to be a reminder of the 56-inch chest, a metaphor for a strong and decisive government.

Manmohan Singh’s ‘mistake’?

Let me first play the devil’s advocate. Aspiring doctors, students, and youth in general need to understand that PM Modi doesn’t speak on anything that is negative about his government. He doesn’t want to repeat the mistakes made by former Prime Minister Manmohan Singh and then-UPA chairperson Sonia Gandhi, who easily buckled under the Opposition’s pressure and yielded to public outrage. Remember how many Union ministers and chief ministers they sacrificed: external affairs minister Natwar Singh over Oil-For-Food scandal; Union home minister Shivraj Patil for 26/11 terror attack—actually for changing his clothes way too often during that crisis; Maharashtra CM Vilasrao Deshmukh for its inept handling—actually for giving a tour of terror-hit Taj to his actor son Riteish and filmmaker Ram Gopal Varma; Deshmukh’s successor Ashok Chavan for the Adarsh scam; Union law minister Ashwani Kumar for alleged interference in a Central Bureau of Investigation probe; and many more.

A senior Congress leader once told me about his conversation with Sonia Gandhi, who apparently conceded to him that asking the Union ministers and CMs to resign was a mistake, as it only made the Opposition more strident. I wouldn’t call it a mistake, though. A democratically elected government must respond to public sentiments even if it has to pay a political cost. The Modi government obviously doesn’t see it this way.

Lakhs of students and their families may be feeling outraged over the NEET-UG paper leak and lapses and irregularities in other examinations. The Modi government won’t, however, yield to their demand for the education minister’s resignation, as it would be a sign of weakness. How did the show of respect for public sentiment serve the Manmohan Singh government? It only made people more demanding and unforgiving, making the UPA government look increasingly weak. The UPA government folded under public support for Anna Hazare’s fast-unto-death within 12 days and yielded to his demand. This laid the foundation for the UPA’s eventual ouster. Do you even remember if the Lokpal exists today?

Anyway, this should explain the Modi government’s refusal to even acknowledge the protests by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and Wangchuk’s three-week-long fast. When it threatened to become a ‘nuisance’ in front of Parliament, the police just bundled Wangchuk out to a hospital. His wife wants to shift him to a private facility, but the authorities won’t let her do that.

The government was obviously taken aback on Monday. It probably didn’t expect students and youth from across the country to move beyond social media and descend on the country’s capital in thousands in support of Wangchuk and the CJP. Health minister JP Nadda had to give an audience to a CJP delegation as the police lathicharged and tear gas didn’t seem to break the morale of young protesters. The only other time the Modi government buckled in the past was when it had to scrap the farm laws due to farmers’ prolonged protests on Delhi’s borders. I am not sure yet if the government finds Monday’s protest electorally alarming enough to make a second exception.

The Modi government needs to do a rethink. Listen to what these young protesters are saying. It’s not just about the NEET paper leak anymore. It’s not even about Dharmendra Pradhan. Among the protesters were teenagers who have passed out of prestigious public schools in the national capital and even got admission in Delhi University. They weren’t affected by the paper leak, but they were coming to Jantar Mantar to do what many of them said was their ‘moral duty’. The government’s refusal to even engage with protesting students and Wangchuk is precisely what has triggered these teenagers and youth. Members of students’ organisations affiliated to some political parties did lend support, and some parties did bring in their supporters, but it would be a mistake for the government to look at the crowds on Delhi roads as the work of the political Opposition.

Bubbling beneath the surface

The NEET paper leak is just the latest trigger. The huge gathering seems to be a cumulative effect of small grievances that have been building up. When protesters talk about the government’s refusal to engage with the youth, they are only voicing their frustration with a system in which they have no say.

Take, for instance, the government’s diktat about the three-language policy in CBSE schools, which stipulates two native Indian languages, with English virtually becoming a foreign language. I have met so many students and parents, including many Modi supporters, who are upset with this imposition. They see it as a virtual imposition of Sanskrit and an exclusion of foreign languages. Say, if a child is studying in a Delhi school, they would opt for Hindi as one of the native languages and English as the third language. As for the second native language, the choice is severely limited. Students may want to opt for Kannada, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali, Gujarati, or Marathi as the second native language. A school would find it difficult to hire teachers for each of these languages. It’s easier to hire a Sanskrit teacher to meet the second native language criterion. And what if students—and their parents—want a foreign language to be taught in the school? They can’t, because the government won’t let them.

Did the government ask these parents and students what they wanted? No. If someone aspires to become a doctor and join King George’s Medical University in Lucknow, they must become a vegetarian first. Because UP governor Anandiben Patel is a vegetarian. While the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leaders went on a non-veg binge before the West Bengal Assembly elections, one of the first things the party did after coming to power was to exclude eggs from mid-day meals in schools. Were the parents consulted? No. One BJP-ruled state after another has been bringing laws to regulate live-in relationships, prescribing fines and imprisonment for not registering. Were the youth—or their parents—asked if they would like the government to pry into their bedrooms? No. People have other grouses, too. To cite just one instance, they don’t know what to do with their cars as the government’s sudden decision to increase ethanol blending to 20 per cent has reduced the vehicles’ mileage and could potentially damage them.

These are just a few of many, many grievances the youth have. They hear just one response from the government: “I am your benefactor. I give your parents free foodgrains, free medical facilities, cash, and what not. Don’t ask questions. We know what’s good for you. Ask not what the government should do for you, but what you can do for us.”

PM Modi may want to rethink such messaging.

DK Singh is Political Editor at ThePrint. H

body:
56 inch Chest with a 26 inch Spine

BJP surrendered to the Cockroach Janata Party. Dharmendra Pradhan resigned. All FIRs against protesters withdrawn. Compensation for NEET victims accepted. Every single demand met. The 37-day protest at Jantar Mantar ended with CJP posting "Cockroaches won. Democracy won."

This did not have to end this way. And one of the main reasons it did is sycophancy.

For those of us who have been following Indian politics long enough, this movie is familiar. We watched it play out with the Congress party over two decades. The script is the same. Only the cast has changed.

Here is how the sycophancy spiral works.

A powerful leader consolidates authority. The people closest to them rise not because of their ability but because of their loyalty. These loyalists tell the leader what the leader wants to hear. Criticism is treated as disloyalty. Disagreement is treated as betrayal. Over time, the leader becomes surrounded by people whose only skill is praise. JP Nadda. Gogoi. Sanjay Jha. Digvijay Singh. Different parties, same species. They thrive not by being strong but by making the leader feel strong.

The problem is not that these people are sycophants. The problem is what sycophancy does to the information flow.

BJP's own supporters have been demanding Pradhan's resignation for months over the NEET examination scandal. Students died by suicide. Parents were devastated. The anger was real, widespread, and legitimate. But the people around Modi told him it was a non-issue. That the noise would die down. That the party's core support would hold. That Pradhan need not resign because resigning would show weakness.

This is what sycophants do. They filter reality. They present the world as the leader wants to see it, not as it is. And the leader, addicted to the dopamine of constant positive feedback, treats any dissonance as noise rather than signal. When you are in a sycophantic spiral, you are so accustomed to praise that even mild criticism feels like an attack. So you default to more praise. More reassurance. More "everything is fine, sir."

Until it is not fine. Until a satirical movement born from a Chief Justice's insult to unemployed youth puts people on the street and forces your Health Minister to sit across from two 20-somethings and accept every demand they put on the table.

Watch the footage of Nadda meeting the CJP representatives. This is India's Health Minister, a senior BJP leader, practically begging for a handshake. This is what sycophancy produces. Not strength. Weakness dressed in a party robes. When the moment demanded firmness, strategic communication, and a genuine engagement with legitimate grievances, the party sent a man whose instinct was to surrender because he had never been trained to fight. He was trained to agree.

Nadda showed BJP's core voters that the 56-inch chest has deputies with 26-inch spines.

This is the real cost. Elections are not won by core voters alone. Core voters will vote BJP no matter what. But elections are won by swing voters. And swing voters are watching. They are watching Nadda fumble. They are watching the party that projects strength act from weakness. They are watching a satirical Instagram movement outmaneuver the most formidable political machine in Indian history.

Even if swing voters are lost, core voters can be demoralized. They may never switch loyalties. But they may not show up at the polling booth. The dissonance for them is real. They signed up for a party that fights. A party that does not bend. When they see their leaders bend on national television, the gap between the party's self-image and its behavior becomes too wide to ignore. They may not articulate it. But the enthusiasm fades. The booth-level energy drops. The margins shrink.

Congress walked this exact path. A formidable force reduced to losing official opposition status within a decade. Not because the public turned against them overnight. But because the sycophants drowned out the grassroots leaders. Because the Digvijay Singhs, Gogois, Mani Shankars and Sanjay Jhas rose while the genuine talent was sidelined. Because the leadership stopped hearing the truth and started hearing only what made them comfortable.

BJP has one structural advantage Congress never had: it is not wedded to a dynasty. It has the RSS's organizational depth. It has a self-correction mechanism. But sycophancy corrodes self-correction. When the leadership structure is infested with weak men who have no real connect or command, the mechanism rusts.

Modi and Shah can clean house. They can replace the Naddas with fighters. They can rebuild the feedback loops that once made BJP the most responsive political organization in the country. But that requires acknowledging that the problem exists. And acknowledging that the problem exists requires hearing it from someone other than a sycophant.

That is the trap. And it is the same trap Congress walked into. And in all likelihood, BJP will continue to walk into.

Mission Accomplished… Protest Called Off! 🎭
Finally, the agitation at Jantar Mantar has come to an end and the protests are called off.
If you watched the evening TV news discussions, the faces of the opposition spokespersons said it all. They looked so disappointed! It almost felt like they were unhappy that the issue got resolved peacefully without creating more chaos. 

For weeks, political parties and groups like CJP were shouting on the streets. 

But let us ask one simple, honest question: Did CJP or any opposition leader give even ONE good, practical suggestion on how to reform NEET or improve the exam system?
The answer is a big NO. 
Zero suggestions
zero plans
zero interest in the real future of the students. 
It was all just political drama to target the Modi government.

While they were busy making noise, look at what the Central Government is actually doing on the ground to protect our students:
 Moving towards Computer-Based Testing (CBT) wherever possible, so physical paper leaks during printing and transport are stopped completely.
 Question papers will be sent directly to exam centers through encrypted digital vaults.
 Using Aadhaar-based biometric verification at centers so no fake candidate or impersonator can enter.
 Deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) to catch suspicious activities and tampered OMR sheets.
 Strengthening cybersecurity with special IT agencies and forming a National Technical Committee to set strict protocols for all competitive exams.
 Enforcing the strict Public Examinations Act 2024, which brings severe punishments—up to 10 years in jail and a ₹10 crore fine for paper leak mafias.
This is the real difference. One side used students for political gain and television attention. The Modi Government, on the other hand, worked silently to bring real, permanent solutions for our youth.
Our students deserve a clean system, not political games! 🤝🇮🇳

body:
The more you analyse why we see so many videos which are abusing the PM especially done by girls the more you realise the protests in the age of Internet are not just protests but a viral moment.

The moment the agitation became viral, it stopped being about NEET and turned into something else entirely. 

In the attention economy, once a cause starts generating high engagement, it acquires a life of its own. For a generation that lives inside social media, visibility itself becomes the reward.

Gen Z does not just use platforms. There lives are on them. Status, identity, and self-worth are increasingly measured in reach, shares, and perceived moral positioning. 

When a protest offers the chance to be seen as righteous, brave, and relevant, the dopamine hit is powerful. 

Each viral video, each round of applause from the online crowd reinforces the behaviour. The cause becomes secondary to the feeling of mattering.

There is also a deeper psychological layer. Young people are naturally more idealistic. They have a stronger need for moral clarity and a lower tolerance for perceived injustice. 

When this idealism collides with the attention economy, protests become very strong. Participating feels both virtuous and rewarding. It satisfies the desire to do something meaningful while simultaneously delivering social validation.

This combination is why the CJP protests gained traction so quickly and proved difficult to contain. It was not just organisational strength or political backing. 

It was the fusion of idealism with a dopamine driven attention system that constantly rewarded escalation and visibility.

This is the new terrain. Protests that successfully plug into the attention economy do not follow the old rules.

India’s Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan Resigns Amid Student Protests

India’s Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan has announced his resignation amid prolonged student protests and political pressure. In a letter posted on the social media platform X (formerly Twitter) on Saturday (July 25), he announced his resignation.
According to various Indian media reports, Dharmendra Pradhan has already submitted his resignation to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Hours after the resignation announcement, a third round of talks was scheduled to take place between the protesting organization Kokroch Janata Party (CJP) and representatives of the central government.

The protesters, who had been staging a sit-in at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar for more than a month, had three major demands. Their primary demand was the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. They also demanded assurances that no legal action would be taken against participating students and compensation of INR 10 million for the families of students who died by suicide following the alleged NEET question paper leak.

Two rounds of talks had previously been held between the government and the protesters, but no agreement was reached over the education minister’s resignation. On Saturday morning, the CJP made it clear that it would not engage in further talks with the government unless Dharmendra Pradhan was removed or resigned.

Against this backdrop, Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation is being viewed as a significant development in the ongoing protest movement.

body:
What did the protest at Jantar Mantar achieve ?
By Justice Katju
The Cockroach Janta Party ( CJP ) protest which began on 19th June 2026 at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, ended on 25th July with the resignation of the Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and acceptance of 2 other demands of the CJP by the government, with great celebration and revelry by the protestors.
What has it achieved ? Nothing, and yet something. Let me explain.
The entire agitation was focused on the demand for resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan. Why ? Because of paper leaks in the NEET examinations
https://t.co/UJD0mRsP3U
But why are there paper leaks ? Because of corruption. Corruption is rampant in India, in almost every sphere, not just in NEET.
So paper leaks will continue as long as corruption continues in India. And corruption will continue in India, as the Anna Hazare anti-corruption movement of 2011 has proved. The movement started with great fanfare, and soon acquired a huge following in India, but later on fizzled out, with nothing achieved. In fact many believe that corruption is even more today, and at every level.
So resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan has only resulted in his replacement by another Education Minister, but it will have no effect in paper leaks, since corruption will continue in India.
So has the CJP protest achieved nothing ? I believe it has achieved something important.
Till now there were 2 narratives prevailing in India.
The first was that India was progressing, with the fastest growing economy in the world and rise in GDP, and had already surpassed Japan and would soon surpass Germany, making the Indian economy the third largest in the world.
https://t.co/NZQTQoWBEm
https://t.co/JVOM8nNhZI
The second was that in fact the Indian economy was stagnant ( if not in recession ), with record and rising unemployment, skyrocketing prices of food and other essential commodities, appalling level of child malnutrition ( every second Indian child is malnourished, according to Global Hunger Index ), almost total lack of proper healthcare and good education for the masses, etc.
https://t.co/xoX5Ugsmve
https://t.co/UMcYHolCE0
https://t.co/jDTWBbOAVz
https://t.co/QtrHWCj9JY
https://t.co/xfso7t7AXZ
https://t.co/PgTKASTMZJ
Many people were confused as to which narrative was correct.
The CJP movement has in a flash removed the confusion, and proved that the second narrative is correct. This became evident when within a few days of creation ( as a satire ) of the CJP its creator Abhijeet Dipke, a student of Boston University, got over 20 million followers
https://t.co/UJD0mRsP3U
The cause of this huge response to the CJP is the massive unemployment in India, which has reached a record level.
12 million youth are entering the job market in India every year, but less than half a million jobs are created annually in the organized sector of the Indian economy. So where do the remaining 11.5 million go ? They become hawkers, street vendors, bouncers, stringers, criminals, beggars, or end up as suicides, and many girls become prostitutes. If a single peon's ( chaprasi ) job is advertised by the government there are usually thousands of applicants, some even with Ph.D. MBA, https://t.co/p6awnfZTgl, or engineering degrees.
The looming spectre of unemployment after they complete their education is in the minds of most Indian youth. This is the real cause of the huge numbers of supporters which the CJP movement has acquired so quickly.
But it is only an emotional response, and will not solve the unemployment problem, nor of paper leaks.
The government has announced that it is bringing a Bill in Parliament for imposing a sentence of upto 10 years imprisonment for those involved in paper leaks.
To my mind this will only give another handle to the police to extort money, as experience has shown.
Moreover, even if paper leaks are checked, it will only mean that meritorious students will get admission instead of non meritorious ones. But it will not increase the number of available jobs in the country.
Jobs can be increased and unemployment largely abolished when the economy is rapidly expanding. But this rapid expansion of the economy is not possible within the present system prevailing in India.
It can only take place after a revolution, following a protracted people's struggle ( jan sangharsh ), rising above caste and religion, led by modern minded leaders, in which tremendous sacrifices will have to be made, and thereafter creating a political and social order under which there is rapid industrialization, and steady rise in the standard of living of the people.
https://t.co/fMtvUccqa7
How to launch such a people's struggle which will culminate in a historical people's revolution, is what our patriotic youth should think of, instead of just shouting and screaming at Jantar Mantar

body:
インド「ゴキブリ人民党（CJP）」の由来を徹底深掘り
先日のYahoo!ニュース投稿で話題になったように、2026年7月25日、インドの教育相ダルメンドラ・プラダン氏が辞任しました。
これを主導したのが、「ゴキブリ人民党」（英語：Cockroach Janta Party、略称CJP）という風刺的な運動体です。
一見シュールな名前ですが、その由来と急成長の背景には、インドの若者たちが抱える深刻な不満と、SNS時代ならではのユーモア戦略が凝縮されています。
以下で、発端から最近の成果までを詳しく掘り下げます。
1. きっかけとなった「最高裁長官の一言」（2026年5月15日）
すべてはここから始まりました。
インド最高裁判所長官のスーリヤ・カント氏が法廷で、失業中の若者や政府批判をする若者を
「ゴキブリ（cockroaches）」や「寄生虫」と表現したと報じられました（本人は「偽の学位を持つ人々を指したもので、若者全体を侮蔑したわけではない」と後日釈明）。
これに激怒したのが、当時米国在住の30歳インド人男性アビジート・ディプケ氏でした。
How Abhijeet Dipke became the face of India's first Gen Z protest movement  - The Japan Times

2. 創設者アビジート・ディプケ氏とは？
30歳（2026年時点）
ボストン大学出身
以前は野党アーム・アードミ党（AAP）のソーシャルメディアチームで活動経験あり（政治コミュニケーション・ストラテジスト）
2026年5月時点で米国在住（その後抗議のため一時帰国）
彼は5月16日、X（旧Twitter）にこう投稿しました：
「全てのゴキブリが集まったとしたらどうなるだろうか？」
その直後、「ゴキブリ人民党（Cockroach Janta Party）」のSNSアカウントと公式サイト（https://t.co/ykiH8BKTk6）を開設。Googleフォームで「党員募集」を開始しました。

3. 党名の由来 ― ただのジョークではない緻密なパロディ
名称の由来は2重構造になっています：
BJPのもじり
与党インド人民党（Bharatiya Janata Party = BJP）を意識的にパロディ化。「Janta（人民）」をそのまま使い、CJPとした。
「ゴキブリ」という言葉の逆転利用
最高裁長官が使った侮蔑語を、自ら名乗ることで毒を抜き、団結の象徴に転換した。
ゴキブリのイメージ（どんな過酷な環境でも生き残る強靭さ）を「若者のレジリエンス（回復力）」に重ねた、非常に洗練された自己卑下ユーモアです。
公式には「若者による、若者のための、若者の政治組織」と位置づけられ、「入党条件は失業者または怠け者」とジョークを交えています（もちろん本気の登録政党ではありません）。

4. 爆発的な拡大の背景
設立からわずか数週間でInstagramフォロワーが2,200万人超に到達。与党BJPの公式アカウントを上回る勢いでした。

へぇ〜ポイント：
インドは世界最大級の若年人口を抱える一方で、若年失業率が深刻。
2026年もNEET（全国共通医学部入試）の試験問題漏洩や、CBSE（中央中等教育委員会）のオンライン採点システム不具合が相次ぎ、数百万人の学生の将来が脅かされた。
これらの不満が「ゴキブリ」という象徴を通じて一気に結集した。

5. オンラインから街頭へ、そして教育相辞任へ
2026年6月6日：ディプケ氏が米国から帰国し、ニューデリーで初の街頭抗議集会を実施（ジャンタル・マンタルで）。
その後、全国規模の座り込み抗議やデモに発展。
抗議の象徴として「金属の皿をスプーンで叩く」パフォーマンスが行われましたが、これは2020年のCOVID禍でモディ首相が呼びかけた「ターリー・バジャオ（皿を叩いて医療従事者を応援）」のパロディでもありました。
そして2026年7月25日、ついに教育相プラダン氏が辞任を表明。CJPは「要求が実現した」として抗議運動の終了を宣言しました。

まとめ：これは「ただのジョーク政党」ではなかった
CJPは公式に登録された政党ではなく、風刺とミームから生まれたGen Z主導の抗議運動です。しかし、その影響力は本物の政治的成果（教育相辞任）を生み出しました。

へぇ〜な事実まとめ：
党のマスコット画像の多くはAI生成。
Xアカウントは一時「国家安全保障上の懸念」でインド国内からアクセス不能にされたが、後日解除。
「ゴキブリ」という最悪の侮蔑語を、最強の結束の象徴に変えた言語戦略の勝利。
この事例は、SNS時代における若者の政治参加の新しい形を世界に示したと言えます。インドの若者たちが「声を出せば変わる」と実感した瞬間でもありました。
もっと詳しく知りたい部分（例：抗議の具体的な手法、ディプケ氏の過去、またはインドの試験制度の闇など）があれば、教えてください！ さらに深掘りします🐹

body:
From One Word to a Nationwide Protest and Education Minister's Resignation, It all began with a single word COCKROACH 🪳 

​After CJI Suryakant allegedly referred to the youth as "cockroaches," the remark triggered outrage across social media. What many viewed as an insult was transformed into a symbol of resistance, leading to the formation of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). Instead of rejecting the label, thousands and later millions embraced it

​Supporters claim that more than 26 million people eventually joined or supported the movement online. What started as a reaction to one controversial remark soon grew into a nationwide campaign demanding accountability and reforms.

​The movement reached a new phase at Jantar Mantar, where students protested over alleged paper leaks. Hunger strikes followed, and as tensions escalated, protesters organized a Sansad March. The march ended in clashes with security forces, with reports of a police lathi-charge and over 100 students reportedly injured.

​As the protests spread across the country, pressure on the government continued to mount. Prime Minister Narendra Modi later released his first public video after the NEET paper leak controversy, but many protesters believed the response had come too late.

​And finally, 83 days after the NEET paper leak and 35 days into the ongoing protests, Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.

​Whether seen as a victory for student activism or simply a political consequence of mounting pressure, the resignation became one of the defining moments of the movement.

​From one word... to a nationwide protest... to a Union Minister's resignation.

body:
The Turning Points That Forced Dharmendra Pradhan’s Resignation

@Cockroachisback , @abhijeet_dipke, @Wangchuk66 , @prakashraaj ,  @AzmiShabana, @SauravDassss 

▶️NEET paper leaks and other exam paper leaks caused endless suffering to lakhs of students. More than 20 students died by suicide due to the NEET paper leak alone.

▶️ CJI called the youth “cockroaches.”  

▶️Abhijeet Dipke from Boston, USA launched the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) online.  

▶️Arun Arora (AAP supporter) in a fun way assigned CJP roles to several known AAP faces. 
 
▶️These volunteers gave the first big push and started trending songs.  

▶️ CJP exploded on Instagram - accounts repeatedly withheld/paused - yet crossed 22 million followers.  

▶️ Abhijeet Dipke announced he was coming to India for the first Jantar Mantar protest (6 June 2026). 
 
▶️ CJP named official spokespersons: Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka, Vijeta Dahiya.  

▶️First Jantar Mantar protest became a massive success. Prakash Raj and Sonam Wangchuk joined, demanding Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation.  

▶️ Protests spread to Pune, Lucknow, Amritsar, Hyderabad, Jaipur and more. Sonam Wangchuk and Prakash Raj kept showing up.  

▶️Opposition parties extended support: AAP, SP, Shiv Sena (UBT), TMC, DMK and others.  

▶️CJP began its indefinite sit-in at Jantar Mantar on 20 June 2026.  

▶️Sonam Wangchuk started his hunger strike at Jantar Mantar on 28 June, demanding Pradhan’s resignation.  Along with him, several students including @neha_aisa too started hunger strike at the site

▶️Student support for CJP grew organically across India.  

▶️ On the 21st day of his hunger strike, police forcibly shifted Sonam Wangchuk to hospital against his will.  

▶️That single mis-step backfired. Support exploded at Jantar Mantar and protests erupted nationwide.  

▶️CJP announced the March to Parliament on 20 July. 2.5 lakh students turned up.  

▶️The entire nation watched in shock as Delhi Police launched a brutal lathi-charge — nails on lathis, RAF pellet guns, shock batons.  

▶️International media extensively covered the police brutality while much of the Indian media ran propaganda branding students as “anti-national.”  

▶️93 former senior civil servants (including a former NSA, former Election Commissioner and former Lt. Governor of Delhi) wrote to the PM condemning the police action.  

▶️ The government thought force would break the movement. Instead, Gen Z became unstoppable.  

▶️ Rahul Gandhi and Congress leaders protested outside the PMO on 21 July.  

▶️People from across India began ordering food and supplies for the protesting students.  

▶️ CJP and AAP launched helplines and secured the release of detained protesters.  Arvind Kejriwal himself went police station after station and got students released. 

▶️Even after being shifted to hospital, Sonam Wangchuk continued his fast. The High Court ordered his transfer to a hospital of his choice (Medanta), yet police still blocked visitors and opposition MPs.  

▶️ On the 26th day, Sonam Wangchuk broke his fast only after receiving written assurances from the Modi government (no FIRs against peaceful protesters, compensation for NEET-related suicide families, and a parliamentary discussion on exam accountability), read out by a BJP minister.  

▶️Nationwide protests on 24 July — “Every district, one day, one demand.”  

▶️The government kept shutting 18 metro stations near Jantar Mantar and blocking roads, punishing ordinary citizens.  

▶️On 25 July, Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.  
The entire nation erupted in joy.

#India’s ‘#Cockroach’ youth movement calls off protests after education minister resigns 

India’s youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has called off its nationwide protests after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned amid mounting anger over alleged examination paper leaks and irregularities.

The resignation on Saturday followed weeks of demonstrations, including a prolonged sit-in at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, demanding accountability over the conduct of major national examinations, particularly the NEET-UG medical entrance test. The protests also drew support from activists and opposition figures and spread to other cities.

The CJP, which began as a satirical online movement in May, evolved into a broader youth protest platform focused on exam reforms, unemployment and government accountability. Its demonstrations intensified after alleged examination irregularities triggered widespread frustration among students and families.

According to the Associated Press and The Guardian, the movement declared victory after Pradhan’s resignation and said it would end its main protests following government assurances on key demands, including compensation for affected families, reforms to prevent exam leaks and protection for peaceful protesters from legal action.

Local media reported the resignation marks a significant political setback for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, coming after sustained public pressure over the education system and examination integrity.

In India, something magnificent happened when young people turned a harsh insult into a historic political victory.

✅During a Supreme Court hearing on May 15, 2026, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant was reprimanding a lawyer over activist litigation. In his remarks, he compared unemployed young people and activists to "COCKROACHES" and "PARASITES of society" who attack state institutions when they fail to find jobs.

✅Instead of slinking away, 30-year-old political communications strategist Abhijeet Dipke launched an online movement the next day called the COCKROACH JANTA PARTY (CJP). Parodying the ruling party (BJP), the CJP adopted the humble cockroach as a mascot, a symbol of resilience, endurance and survival.

✅The movement went viral instantly. Within two weeks, CJP’s Instagram page amassed over 20 million followers, outpacing the official accounts of India’s main political parties.

✅The Boiling Point: Exam Scandals:
The satire transformed into a massive real-world protest when paper leaks invalidated major competitive national entrance exams (such as NEET-UG). Millions of students saw years of hard work shattered.

✅The youth took to the streets, occupying New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and organizing nationwide sit-ins. Renowned environmentalist and education activist Sonam Wangchuk  joined forces with the youth, embarking on a 26-day hunger strike. The movement set a single non-negotiable demand: 

❌the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan❌

✅On July 25, 2026, after sustained nationwide pressure, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan officially submitted his resignation to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

✅Why this was historic: 
Prime Minister Modi's administration has long maintained a strongman image, famously refusing to force or accept minister resignations during major public protests. The youth movement achieved a political concession that few thought possible.
