body:
🚨CJP Ends 37-Day Protest After Government Accepts Key Demands, Raising New Questions for India's Democracy

The 37-day nationwide protest led by the CJP formally came to an end after a joint press conference with government representatives, where the organisation announced that its primary objectives had been achieved and instructed protesters to vacate Jantar Mantar and return home peacefully.

According to CJP leaders, the movement was built around three core demands: the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, the withdrawal of FIRs filed against protesters and organisers, and financial compensation for families who allegedly lost loved ones following the NEET paper leak controversy.

The first demand was fulfilled with Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. The government also reportedly assured the protesters that FIRs related to the agitation would be withdrawn and that future legal action against peaceful participants would not be pursued. On compensation, the government is said to have agreed to provide the maximum assistance permissible under existing provisions to affected families. CJP stated that these assurances were made in writing, prompting it to withdraw the agitation in what it described as an act of "good faith."

The protest's conclusion marks a significant political moment. It is being viewed as one of the rare instances in recent years where sustained public mobilisation coincided with the resignation of a Union minister. While the opposition had consistently demanded the minister's removal inside Parliament, much of the political credit is likely to be associated with the street movement rather than parliamentary pressure.

At the same time, the government's reported assurance to withdraw FIRs has sparked debate over its long-term implications. Critics argue that withdrawing cases linked to a mass protest could establish a precedent that future movements, regardless of their nature, may seek to invoke. They contend that allegations involving violence or damage to public property are ordinarily expected to be addressed through the judicial process rather than political negotiations. Supporters, however, maintain that many protesters faced legal action despite participating peacefully and believe the withdrawal is necessary to prevent unnecessary criminalisation of dissent.

During the course of the protest, concerns were also raised over misinformation circulating on social media, including claims that several foreign and Pakistani-linked accounts amplified misleading narratives surrounding the movement. While such allegations became part of the public discourse, there has been no conclusive evidence to suggest that they altered the overall course of the agitation.

With the protest now officially withdrawn, attention is expected to shift back to Parliament, where several important legislative measures remain pending. The episode leaves behind a lasting political and constitutional debate over the role of protests, government accountability, legal processes, and the future relationship between street activism and democratic institutions.

The 2021 NEET-PG counselling movement was one of the biggest nationwide protests by resident doctors in India.

Led by the 𝙁𝙚𝙙𝙚𝙧𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙤𝙛 𝙍𝙚𝙨𝙞𝙙𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝘿𝙤𝙘𝙩𝙤𝙧𝙨' 𝘼𝙨𝙨𝙤𝙘𝙞𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 (𝙁𝙊𝙍𝘿𝘼) along with other resident doctors' associations, thousands of doctors across India protested against the prolonged delay in NEET-PG counselling and admissions.

At that time, the 𝙐𝙣𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙃𝙚𝙖𝙡𝙩𝙝 𝙈𝙞𝙣𝙞𝙨𝙩𝙚𝙧 𝙬𝙖𝙨 𝙈𝙖𝙣𝙨𝙪𝙠𝙝 𝙈𝙖𝙣𝙙𝙖𝙫𝙞𝙮𝙖. The doctors demanded immediate counselling, timely recruitment of new residents, and relief from the excessive workload caused by the shortage of doctors in hospitals.

The protest intensified in December 2021, with demonstrations across the country and disruption of services in several government hospitals. Representatives of FORDA and other doctors' bodies held discussions with the Health Ministry, after which assurances were given to expedite the counselling process.

Following the government's assurances and the Supreme Court proceedings, the resident doctors called off their strike in January 2022, while continuing to monitor the implementation of the commitments.

This movement highlighted the vital role of resident doctors in India's healthcare system and the need for timely medical recruitment and better healthcare planning.

body:
After weeks of protests, sleepless nights and a march to Parliament, the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has finally called off its agitation at Delhi's Jantar Mantar.

The announcement came after a fresh round of talks with the Centre, with the government agreeing to the movement's key demands, including the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. CJP leaders then appealed to supporters to peacefully disperse and begin returning home, saying the protest had achieved its objective.

The mood at Jantar Mantar changed almost instantly.

The roads around the protest site, which had witnessed barricades, police deployment and tense stand-offs over the past several weeks, turned into scenes of celebration. Supporters danced to music, chanted slogans, showered flower petals, embraced one another and celebrated what they described as a victory for the student movement. Drums, songs and cheers echoed through the streets surrounding Jantar Mantar as thousands marked the end of the agitation.

The Centre has also agreed to several other demands raised by the movement, including measures related to examination reforms, compensation for families of students whose deaths the movement linked to NEET, withdrawal of cases against peaceful protesters and assurances that no action would be taken against students who participated in the demonstrations.

Opposition parties, which had backed the protests over the past several weeks, welcomed the developments while maintaining that the police action during the 20 July crackdown must also be accounted for.

After more than a month, the protest site that became the epicentre of one of the country's biggest student-led movements is finally beginning to empty—but only after ending on a celebratory note.

The Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) has officially called off its protest at Jantar Mantar following discussions with government representatives.

This comes after Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan submitted his resignation earlier in the day. 

Speaking after a meeting at the Constitution Club of India, CJP leaders announced that the protest would not continue for now while also presenting a five-point charter outlining their remaining demands. 

These include compensation for families of students who died by suicide in connection with the NEET paper leak controversy, the release of detained students and protesters, and no fresh FIRs against those involved.

From the ground, people were seen leaving the protest site as metro stations reopened, though some participants continued to express support for the movement and its demands.

body:
🌈 My thoughts on the NEET protest :

📎 1. I have stayed largely silent on the NEET agitation out of deference to those closer to events. My concern has been less political and more about the need for lasting examination reform.

📎2. It is welcome that the Government has engaged with the students' concerns and responded with empathy to key demands.

📎3. Credit is also due to the CJP and its leadership for keeping the movement largely restrained and articulate despite strong criticism from different people and TV anchors.

📎4. The next challenge is implementation. A law alone is not enough; it must be backed by a time-bound investigation that fixes accountability and restores public trust.

📎5. Dr. Radhakrishnan's 2024 recommendations after the first NEET leak were sound. The question in 2026 is not what more needs to be recommended, but why those recommendations were not implemented.

📎6. Basic questions remain unanswered. Who selected the paper setters, from what pool, under what SOP, and who approved those selections? These answers should not have to wait for fresh recruitment into the NTA. They should already be known and made public. Because it matters more than nabbing the  leakers.

📎7. In 2024, the breach involved tampering with question paper boxes. In 2026, it appears to involve an insider leak linked to paper setters. If so, identifying the approval chain is critical to determine whether the failure arose from negligence, incompetence or corruption.

📎8. Finally, the use of lathis, indiscriminate RAF firing, and organised stone-pelting at protest sites all deserve condemnation. In a democracy, neither excessive force nor organised violence is acceptable. The real test is whether this crisis produces a more credible examination system and a more mature handling of public order.

I hope one can see changes which show on the ground - not only in courtrooms and behind closed doors.  meetings

STORY | CJP calls off protest as government accepts all demands

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Saturday withdrew its agitation over the NEET issue after the government accepted all demands of the outfit, including the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and withdrawal of FIRs against protesters.

The announcement came following talks between the two sides soon after Pradhan said on X that he has sent his resignation to the prime minister.

Union Minister JP Nadda said the government will give "honourable compensation" within rules to the families of the students who committed suicide after the NEET test cancellation and ensure withdrawal of all FIRs registered against the protesters.

"As the government accepted all our demands, we call off our protests with immediate effect. We appeal to everyone to go back home peacefully," CJP's spokesperson Saurav Das said at a joint press conference with Nadda and Union Minister Jitendra Singh.

The CJP has led a sit-in at Jantar Mantar since June 20, demanding accountability over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak and irregularities in the CBSE's on-screen marking process, besides seeking wider reforms in the conduct of public examinations.

The agitation has galvanised thousands of students in protests across the country and has been supported by major opposition parties.

Sonam Wangchuk never demanded anyone’s head he ended his hunger strike after assurances, showing pragmatism.

Yet CJP’s Abhijit Dipke and his outfit refuse to back down, desperately clinging to their agitation because their real agenda was never just NEET reforms it was political disruption and scoring points against a strong government.

This isn’t student advocacy; it’s selective outrage and opportunistic politics dressed up as protest.

While genuine concerns over exam leaks deserve accountability and systemic fixes, CJP’s refusal to accept reality exposes their hypocrisy.

Pradhan served with dedication on education reforms; bowing to sustained pressure doesn’t erase his contributions or validate endless vendettas. 

Wangchuk moved on why can’t Dipke and CJP? 

Their agitation was always more about optics and pressure tactics than solutions.

Time to focus on real governance, not performative politics that hold India’s youth hostage.

body:
Before BJP IT Cell floods your feed with...
"Modi Masterstroke."
Let's call it what it looks like.
A "Stupidstroke."

Dharmendra Pradhan had to go.
No debate.

India's education system is rotten.
It needed surgery.

Not slogans.
Not committees.
Not another press conference.

A complete overhaul.

But timing is everything.

The government did not remove him after reform.
It removed him after pressure.

And that changes everything.

CJP had no proven national student base.
No moral legitimacy to dictate terms to the Government.

Yet this government served legitimacy to it...
On a silver platter.

Now they can proudly say:
"We forced a Union Minister to resign."

Congratulations!!!

You have just manufactured a political brand.

Tomorrow...
A political party.
A pressure cartel.
An unelected veto machine.

A B-team of AAP that quietly slices BJP's own vote bank.

BJP has seen this movie before.

It surrendered the Farm Laws.
Now it has surrendered a Minister.

Not because accountability was wrong.

But because the street learnt something far more dangerous.

Pressure works.
Or worse...
Violence works.

That is the real headline.

Once a protest tastes blood...
It doesn't ask for dessert.
It asks for the kitchen.

Today...
Dharmendra Pradhan.

Tomorrow...
Action against the police.

Then another Minister.
Then the Home Minister.

Eventually...
Narendra Modi.

What a Masterstroke.

Bravo.

You didn't end the protest.
You upgraded its business model.

When governments reward pressure...
Pressure becomes policy.

When governments reward street muscle...
Street muscle becomes strategy.

And when survival becomes more important than reform...
Reform is the first casualty.

The tragedy is this.

Nobody will now discuss NEET reforms.
Nobody will discuss NTA reforms.
Nobody will discuss paper leaks.
Nobody will discuss fixing the system.

The system disappears.
The spectacle survives.

CJP has not ended.
It has just learnt one lesson.

The Government can be made to kneel.

धर्मेंद्र प्रधान का इस्तीफ़ा बताता है कि देश में छात्रों, युवाओं और GenZ के संघर्ष ने अहंकारी – तानाशाही मोदी सरकार को झुका दिया।
राष्ट्रपति जी को अब तुरंत प्रभाव से यह इस्तीफ़ा स्वीकार कर लेना चाहिए।

राहुल गांधी जी के नेतृत्व में कांग्रेस पार्टी पिछले कई साल से सड़क से लेकर संसद तक education system में सुधार के समर्थन और Paper Leak के विरोध में आवाज़ उठा रही है। मुझे गर्व है कि इस आंदोलन में भी @INCIndia पार्टी ने ज़िम्मेदार विपक्ष की भूमिका निभाई।

‘छात्रों की गूंज’ के तहत देश के स्टूडेंट्स को एकजुट किया, प्रधान मंत्री आवास के बाहर मजबूती के साथ धरना दिया गया, LOp को पुलिस हिरासत में लिया गया और कांग्रेस, @nsui, @IYC सहित हमारे सभी संगठनों ने पूरी मजबूती के साथ इस लड़ाई को लड़ा।

NEET Paper Leak के बाद से Congress Party इस मांग पर डटी रही कि education minister के resignation से कम कुछ मंजूर नहीं है। @RahulGandhi जी ने आज सुबह भी कहा था कि नरेंद्र मोदी अब इस देश का अतीत बन चुके हैं, हमारे ये बच्चे और स्टूडेंट्स देश का भविष्य हैं और अतीत कभी भविष्य को नहीं हरा सकता।

जिस तरह से जंतर मंतर पर महीने भर से अधिक समय से देश भर के students इकट्ठे हुए, GenZ एकजुट हुए, innovative और शांतिपूर्ण तरीके से इस सड़ी हुई व्यवस्था के खिलाफ़ अपना आक्रोश जाहिर किया। इस पूरे दौरान CJP और तमाम संगठनों, विपक्षी दलों ने जो एकजुटता दिखाई; वह काबिल-ए-तारीफ़ है। देशभर की छात्रशक्ति के collective efforts से इस शासन का घमंड टूटा है।

20 जुलाई 2026 का दिन फिर भी कभी भुलाया नहीं जाएगा। जिस तरह से देश के बच्चों पर, GenZ पर सरकार की शय पर बर्बरता की गई, लाठीचार्ज किया गया, आँसू गैस के गोले दागे गए, पैलेट गन चलाई गई, वह सब मोदी सरकार का एक अक्षम्य अपराध है, जिसे कभी माफ़ नहीं किया जाएगा।

छात्रों के आंदोलन को कुचलने के लिए इस सरकार ने क्या कुछ नहीं किया ?
पूरी दिल्ली को एक तरह से lock कर दिया, 17 - 18 मेट्रो स्टेशन बंद कर दिए, जंतर मंतर और आसपास कई किलोमीटर तक internet बंद कर दिया, पुलिस की सख्ती बढ़ा दी गई और इन दिनों तो protest site पर food और water delivery भी रोक दी गई थी। यह खुले तौर पर देशवासियों के fundamental rights और human rights पर हमला है।

20 जुलाई को छात्रों के साथ जो हिंसा की गई, उसकी जाँच की जानी चाहिए, ज़िम्मेदारी तय की जाए। गृह मंत्री और प्रधान मंत्री इस देश से अपने कुकर्मों के लिए माफ़ी मांगे। संसद में शिक्षा व्यवस्था में सुधारों पर सकारात्मक रूप से चर्चा की जाए और पेपर लीक के तनाव के कारण देश के जिन होनहार स्टूडेंट्स ने अपनी जान दे दी, उनके परिवारों की मदद की जाए।

देश के युवाओं, GenZ और स्टूडेंट्स के समर्थन में, education system को सुधारने के लिए हमारा संघर्ष हमेशा जारी रहेगा।✊🏻

Dipke knew this. His own Vijeta Dahiya and Arpit Sharma are reel makers. They knew their playground already. The easiest way to pull Gen Z into the streets was through Instagram where every moment could become a reel.

Look closely. The videos getting the most likes from the CJP protest are from influencers(not students) whose next videos are about hitting 100M views or 100K followers overnight and not about the NEET exam.

Just like TikTok..BJP needs to find a reason to ban Instagram and these reel making platforms so students can concentrate on studies/exams instead of chasing viral fame in protests.

body: One thing that I can vouch for is GOI is NOT chutiya, there is a contingency plan! Also, If you do an indept analysis of the letter from Dharmendra Pradhan you will observe that the document is designed as a trap for the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) rather than a straightforward concession. By publishing the text directly as unformatted image cards on social media without an official letterhead, seal or wet-ink signature, Pradhan has successfully bypassed traditional bureaucratic routing to execute a populist maneuver. This lack of institutional insignia is a calculated tactical choice that transforms an administrative exit into an unfiltered emotional appeal directly to the public base. The text front-loads administrative accountability by meticulously detailing the May 3 NEET-UG disruptions, the subsequent CBI investigation, the June 21 re-examination, and the structural pivot to Computer-Based Testing (CBT), thereby establishing a preemptive defense that the state moved swiftly to correct system failures. By pivoting to complain that individuals in responsible positions created hurdles following the July 16 results, the narrative introduces an ambiguous villain that shifts public anger away from the ministry itself. The core of the trap for the CJP lies in the text's explicit invocation of the protests at Jantar Mantar and its warning against anti-national forces. By framing the resignation as an altruistic sacrifice designed to keep student futures out of legal complexities and to neutralize national security vulnerabilities the document acts as tactical jujitsu against the movement. It presents the CJP leadership with a severe strategic dilemma if the movement declares victory and demobilizes, it loses its momentum, but if it stays on the streets to push secondary demands, state and media apparatuses can reframe the protest as an intractable, politically motivated disruption rather than a student-led welfare campaign.

body:
First, let's give the students their due. 

They pushed, and a Union minister is gone. That does not happen often in this country.

Dharmendra Pradhan has resigned as Education Minister today, sending his letter to the Prime Minister, in the middle of the nationwide protests over the NEET-UG paper leak. 

This came just hours after reports that the government was only planning to shift him to another ministry. 

So the street did the resignation.

This is a pattern with this government.

When the farmers sat on Delhi's borders for a year, the three farm laws were repealed. When the lateral entry recruitment ad drew backlash in 2024, it was pulled. And now, after weeks of protest, a minister has stepped down.

Say what you want about the politics. A government that climbs down when the public pushes hard enough is democracy actually working. 

The pressure is supposed to travel upward like this. And given the chaos, stepping him down was the right call.

The protests had shut 18 Delhi Metro stations and brought real disruption to the capital, with students at Jantar Mantar and Sonam Wangchuk on a hunger strike. 

When a situation is that hot, removing the lightning rod cools it fast. It buys everyone room to breathe.

But, to be honest, a resignation solves almost nothing about the actual problem.

Remember how this leak even happened. The paper did not walk out of a broken vault. It came from an insider, a subject expert the NTA itself had appointed, who recalled the questions and passed them on. 

A new minister in the chair does not touch that. He does not change the press, the storage room, or the panel of experts who see the paper before the students do.

And we already learned that a tough law alone does not stop this. The anti-paper-leak law with ten-year jail terms was on the books in 2024. The paper still leaked in 2026. Punishment on paper did not prevent it.

So if the resignation is the headline, the actual solution is the Centre is moving NEET to a computer-based test format from next year. 

It has set up an STF and fast-track courts with day-to-day trials, and it has proposed seven key amendments to the anti-paper-leak law. This sits on top of the earlier steps, the CBI probe, the cancelled exam, and the re-test whose results came on 16 July.

A computer-based test with a secure, randomised question bank is far harder to leak than a single printed paper trucked to thousands of centres. 

But the 2024 law was announced too, and it failed in practice. So the only thing worth watching now is execution. 

> Does the CBT rollout actually stay secure.
> Do the fast-track courts hand down real sentences. 
> Does the expert-selection process genuinely change. 

Announcements are easy but none of them stop a leak by themselves.

Two more honest things;

This was late. Pradhan's resignation was being demanded back in the 2024 NEET row, by opposition parties and student groups alike. 

He did not go then. It took a second leak, a bigger crisis, and a student movement on the streets to force it now. 

And it did not even end the protest. The CJP called it a partial victory and laid out two more demands before they stop, a one crore compensation for the families of students who died by suicide during this crisis, and disciplinary action against the police for the force used on protesters on 20 July. 

In my opinion, the only number that actually matters is whether a paper leaks next May. 

If the CBT shift and the court cases and the NTA overhaul are done properly, this becomes a real turning point. If they stay as press notes, we will be back here in two years with a new minister and the same hole in the wall.

The reform is the test.

“We are cockroaches; once it enters, it does not leave.”

Following the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG paper leak controversy, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke made it clear at Jantar Mantar that the student movement is far from over.

Addressing the crowd after news of the minister's exit broke, Dipke emphasized that while Pradhan's resignation marks a massive victory for student accountability, the CJP will not clear the protest site until its remaining key demands are met—including ₹1 crore compensation for the families of students who died by suicide amid exam stress, and full accountability for police actions during earlier demonstrations.

We are deeply concerned by multiple reports reaching us of students and other protestors being targeted, detained, or arrested by various state agencies, particularly in Assam, West Bengal, and Bihar.

The Cockroach Janta Party had called off its nationwide protest only after the Government of India assured us that no punitive action would be taken against any protestor, either now or in the future, in any BJP-ruled or NDA-ruled states. First, we wish to assure every protestor that our legal team is already coordinating with brilliant lawyers in the concerned states to secure the release of those detained and to extend all possible legal assistance. This has been happening from Day 1.

Second, we call upon the Government of India, particularly @JPNadda ji and @DrJitendraSingh ji, to immediately honour the assurance given to us by ensuring the release of those detained and by directing that no coercive or retaliatory action is taken against any protestor anywhere in the country. The FIRs registered ought to be withdrawn too.

The Government of India is also reminded of its commitment to furnish us the written guarantee in this regard by tomorrow, Tuesday, 28 July 2026.

Our decision to suspend the nationwide protest was taken in good faith and solely on the basis of the government’s assurance that it would stand by its word. Any departure from that assurance would not merely amount to a breach of trust with the Cockroach Janta Party but would also be a breach of public trust with lakhs of young Indians who chose dialogue over protests.

Such breach of trust will be completely unacceptable to the youth.

The Government of India is reminded that it derives credibility not from just making a promise, but from the promises they honour.

CJP is celebrating the resignation of the Education Minister as some great "victory."

But ask them one simple question—how does one man's resignation fix systemic exam leaks or create a foolproof system?

They have no answer.

Most of them don't even know about the Radhakrishnan Committee or its recommendations. Why? Because they never wanted real, long-term solutions. They only wanted a political scalp.

This entire protest was never about education reform. It was a carefully orchestrated, politically motivated agitation backed by AAP, certain extremists, and the usual left-liberal gang whose only real agenda is to abuse Modi day and night.

Vulgar language, open hate, and pure political opportunism dressed up as student anger.

Resignation is not the solution. Structural reform is. And these people were never interested in that.

Here's the accurate data on the number of medical colleges and MBBS seats in India:

In 2014: • 387 medical colleges • 51,348 MBBS seats

In 2026: • 844 medical colleges • 1,39,489 MBBS seats

The number of medical colleges has more than doubled.

MBBS seats have nearly tripled.

This is real capacity building—not just slogans or protests demanding resignations.

While some are busy shouting for political optics, the actual expansion of medical education has been historic.

While you are criticising the government for not doing anything, you should first look at the numbers above.

Now let's come to the main argument.

According to me, the Education Minister should resign not because the NEET paper leak happened, as he had no direct role in it. It was carried out by paper setters and the coaching mafia.

However, he should resign for not implementing the Radhakrishnan Committee's recommendations in full.

The Radhakrishnan Committee's 101 recommendations are more than an anti-paper leak roadmap—they're a blueprint to rebuild trust in India's examination system.

Key reforms include:

🔹 Encrypted digital question paper delivery, printed only minutes before the exam.

🔹 Aadhaar + biometric + AI-based multi-stage candidate verification to curb impersonation.

🔹 AI-driven detection of cheating, suspicious score patterns, and malpractice.

🔹 Around 1,000 secure government testing centres with CCTV, mobile jammers, and standardised infrastructure.

🔹 Gradual shift to Computer-Based and Adaptive Testing.

🔹 Stronger cybersecurity, reduced outsourcing, dedicated vigilance and research wings, better grievance redressal, and mental health support.

The committee correctly identified that paper leaks aren't isolated failures—they're symptoms of systemic weaknesses across the entire exam lifecycle.

The solution, therefore, isn't just harsher punishment; it's structural reform through technology, governance, and accountability.

If implemented effectively, these reforms could significantly reduce paper leaks, improve transparency, restore public confidence, and modernise the examination process for the 2+ crore students who appear for competitive exams every year.

Now the real challenge is ensuring these recommendations move from paper to practice.

Dear @narendramodi @PMOIndia @dpradhanbjp @JoshiPralhad 🙏

Just heard an interesting conversation near the lift lobby of my apartment.

A few girls were talking about the NEET protest. One of them said, "Look at the NEET protest by CJP. They got justice by forcing the Education Minister to resign." Another added, "The Education Minister doesn't even know how to write a resignation letter."

One of the girls recognised me and said, "Sorry, uncle. We didn't mean anything bad." Then she asked, "Uncle, what do you think?"

By then, the lift had arrived and we all got in.

I just told her, "Never believe the first piece of information you receive on any app. Verify it. Read more. Dig deeper. See who is saying it, what their background is, and what kind of language they themselves have used in public. After that, form your own opinion. The decision is yours."

My floor arrived, and I stepped out.

That conversation stayed with me.

We can criticise people we disagree with, and everyone has the right to question public figures. But what worries me more is how quickly misinformation and propaganda spread through social media. Many young people end up believing the first version of a story they see without checking if it is even true.

At that age, it is easy to believe that every movement is a revolution and that every resignation is the solution to a problem. Real life is much more complicated than that.

The bigger concern is that we are slowly losing our children to misinformation. They deserve facts, not manipulation.

So instead of ignoring them or shouting at them, let us talk to them. Encourage them to question, verify, and think for themselves.

That is our responsibility as parents, elders, teachers, and as a society.

body:
A viral video showing a man in Muslim attire attempting to throw a burning matchstick into the fuel tank of a damaged Mahindra Thar has been falsely shared on social media as footage from the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protest in Delhi, according to an Fact Check investigation.

The video, circulated after the July 20 Parliament march, was shared with claims that it showed a CJP supporter trying to set a vehicle on fire during the protest.

However, Fact Check found that the claim is false. The incident actually took place in Gaya, Bihar, and was unrelated to the NEET protest or the CJP demonstrations.

Using reverse image search, the fact-check team traced the same video to Instagram posts published by CNN-News18 and Moneycontrol on July 18, where it was identified as an incident that occurred following a road accident in Bihar.

According to a Dainik Bhaskar report cited by India Today, a Mahindra Thar collided with a motorcycle and an auto-rickshaw in Gaya, leaving two motorcyclists seriously injured.

Eyewitnesses reportedly claimed that the vehicle bore a BJP sticker and that a woman was driving it, although police did not officially confirm either allegation.

City SDPO Saroj Kumar only confirmed that two persons were injured in the accident and were undergoing treatment.

India Today's local stringer further confirmed that the incident occurred near the Gaya Civil Lines Police Station on July 16.

After the accident, a crowd gathered and some anti-social elements allegedly began pelting stones before attempting to set the vehicle ablaze.

Police later brought the situation under control and registered cases against both the owner and driver of the vehicle, as well as those accused of trying to burn it.

The misleading claim was also amplified by Republic Kannada news anchor Ranjith Shiriyara, who shared the same video multiple times on his social media accounts.

The posts presented the Bihar incident as being connected to the CJP-led NEET protest, despite the video later being fact-checked as unrelated to the Delhi demonstrations.

Meanwhile, the fact-check has gained significance after BJP MLC C.T. Ravi, who recently came under fire for his remarks about "mullahs" during a BJP protest over the NEET controversy in Chikkamagaluru, claimed at a press conference that his comments were made in reference to this viral video.

Ravi had earlier remarked, "What does a mullah have to do with the NEET examination? Even if you tear open his chest, you won't find three letters written there," drawing criticism.

Following a complaint alleging that the speech promoted communal hatred, Chikkamagaluru Town Police registered an FIR against him under provisions relating to promoting enmity and hate speech.

After the FIR was registered, Ravi told reporters that he was referring to the viral video showing a Muslim man trying to set a vehicle on fire and had questioned why such a person would be associated with the NEET protests.

However, the Fact Check establishes that the video Ravi referred to was not from the Delhi protest and had no connection with the CJP agitation.

Instead, it depicted an unrelated incident of mob violence following a traffic accident in Gaya, Bihar. The claim linking the video to the NEET protests was false.

The misleading claim was also amplified by Republic Kannada news anchor Ranjith Shiriyara, who shared the same video multiple times on his social media accounts.

The posts presented the Bihar incident as being connected to the CJP-led NEET protest, despite the video later being fact-checked as unrelated to the Delhi demonstrations.
#FactCheck

STORY | Anti paper leak bill with stricter punishment introduced in Lok Sabha

Government on Monday introduced a bill in the Lok Sabha to amend the anti-paper leaks law with stricter punishment of up to 10 years in jail and a Rs 50 lakh fine, within days of large-scale student protests against the NEET fiasco rocking the nation that forced Dharmendra Pradhan to resign as education minister.

The proposed legislation was introduced by Minister of State for PMO Jitendra Singh amidst protests and sloganeering by the Opposition demanding a response from the government over the police crackdown on students during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)-led July 20 protest march to Parliament.

According to the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, investigations into paper leak cases are to be completed within two months.

The bill says that individuals involved in paper leaks or unfair means in exams will get jail terms for a minimum of 5 years and a maximum of 10 years and a fine of up to Rs 50 lakh.

For organised crimes, the bill proposes a minimum sentence of seven years and a fine of up to Rs 10 crore.

body:
Taking note of a plea on the use of metallic pellet guns during the recent students' protests against the NEET paper leak in Delhi, Supreme Court on Thursday asked Centre to preserve ammunition log of RAF deployed at Jantar Mantar.

Observing that police, as per  Bureau of Police Research and Development (BPRD) advisory, are empowered to use pellet guns in exceptional situations, top court termed “vague” the prayer in the plea seeking a complete ban on such usage.

A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana took note of submissions of senior advocate Vrinda Grover.

Former Central Information Commissioner and retired IPS officer Yashovardhan Azad and the two victims had moved court seeking a complete ban on use of metallic pellet guns to deal with law and order situations.

At theoutset, Justice Bagchi said that the prayer for a ban on the use of pellet guns by law enforcement agencies for civilian crowd dispersal was "vague" without challenging the police regulations, which permit the use of such weapons.

Grover said it was not easy to find such regulations in the public domain, and urged the bench to direct the Centre to place them on record.

Singh and Mansoori reportedly suffered pellet injuries during the ‘Sansad Chalo’ march called by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on July 20.

Grover said as regards the petitioners, metallic pellets were used, and they were recovered from their bodies.

“I am not saying pellet guns should not be in the armoury of the RAF or not. Here it is different. They have used metallic pellets,” she said.

The bench said it was not averse to examining the use of pellets in a particular incident and the petitioners must show if it was permissible under a "graded approach".

The senior lawyer said she was confining her reliefs to metallic pellets.

"There is no standing order of the Delhi Police which permits the use of pellets. That is why my difficulty arises, and I have to rely on BPRD. If there is such a standing order, the Union may place it on record. I am sure the Union and the Delhi Police do not wish to fire pellets on innocent youngsters,” she said.

“I could not find any such standing order of the Delhi Police at all," Grover said.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said the government will do whatever is necessary to assist the bench.

Grover said the top court on July 28 directed the preservation of CCTV, drone, body camera footage and wireless logs and did not specifically refer to ammunition logs of the RAF.

“Whatever is required for investigation will be preserved,” solicitor general said.

The bench said a bona fide protest may turn violent at any point, perhaps due to the infiltration of anti-social elements, and “graded responses” by law enforcement might sometimes be necessary.

The forces may have to take on the spot decision based on the event, the law officer said.

Yashovardhan Azad approached the top court seeking a nationwide ban on the use of wholly or partly metallic pellet ammunition fired from pump-action or projectile action guns for dispersing civilian assemblies, contending that such weapons are inherently incompatible with constitutional standards governing the use of force.

The petition also sought exemplary compensation, comprehensive medical treatment and rehabilitation for all persons allegedly injured in the incident.

According to petition, RAF, deployed to assist Delhi Police in crowd management during protests, resorted to tear gas, lathi-charge and subsequently fired pump-action guns loaded with metallic pellets near Connaught Place.

The petitioners alleged that no prior warning or announcement was issued before the escalation in use of force and that several protesters suffered serious injuries, including eye injuries.

body:
A Conversation That Confirmed What I Was Already Thinking.

This morning, my phone rang. The caller is a hardcore NCP, Congress, and Shiv Sena (UBT) sympathiser who also holds an important organisational position in one of the MVA parties.

After the usual greetings, our conversation naturally shifted to the ongoing NEET protests—the aftermath, why they happened, and what they could mean for the BJP now.

Let me make one thing clear: he is an MVA sympathiser. Yet what he said echoed almost exactly what had been running through my own mind.

Last week, I had written that the BJP's political calculations had gone badly wrong in the NEET paper leak issue. The matter escalated to the point where the Prime Minister had to release three videos, a Union Minister resigned, and the government found itself on the defensive.

First, the BJP has historically been quick to recognise public sentiment and respond when the mood on the streets becomes impossible to ignore. That does not mean it will now bow to every protest. If anything, this episode should encourage the government to become more transparent, accountable, and proactive. Secondly, So those of you, expecting now protests will be the next big thing all the time, dream on!

The next issue brewing up is the ethanol controversy 

Tehseen Poonawalla has raised questions that deserve answers, and it increasingly appears that Nitin Gadkari could become the next political target. Unlike former Union Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, Gadkari has had a much longer public and political career, giving opponents far more material to scrutinise. Whether that translates into anything substantial remains to be seen.

Coming back to my conversation, the MVA sympathiser told me something I completely agreed with.

He said:

"Vikrant, even many people on the Right did not like what happened during these protests. Even many of the Right too supported the students and demanded transparency, but the abusive attacks on the Prime Minister, the assault on policemen, and the destruction of public property crossed the line."

I agreed.

The genuine students who sparked this movement should never become collateral damage. If peaceful students have faced punitive action, the government should review those cases and withdraw action wherever appropriate.

Interestingly, CJP founder Dipke himself acknowledged that anti-India elements and disruptive groups had infiltrated the protests to hijack a legitimate student movement.

What Exactly Is CJP's Objection?

Dipke had earlier stated that those responsible for violence, abusive slogans, and unlawful acts were outsiders who did not represent his supporters.

If that is indeed the case, then shouldn't CJP support action against those specific individuals instead of opposing the entire law enforcement process?

Those who attacked police personnel, vandalised public property, or attempted to derail a peaceful student movement should face the law. Innocent students, however, should be protected.

If CJP itself accepts that anti-social elements infiltrated the protests, then why is it now objecting to the government's action against those accused of violence?

That is a question that deserves an answer.

A New Lease of Life for the Opposition in Maharashtra? 

There is little doubt that this episode has injected fresh energy into an opposition that had appeared politically dormant, particularly in Maharashtra. Dipke has, for the moment, given it a rallying point.

However, Maharashtra is a politically unique state.

Many opposition parties may now attempt to replicate this strategy through younger leaders such as Aaditya Thackeray and Rohit Pawar. But there is one major difference.

People are still trying to understand who Dipke is. Leaders such as Aaditya Thackeray, Rohit Pawar, Uddhav Thackeray, and Raj Thackeray are already familiar political faces. Voters have watched them for years and have largely formed their opinions.

For that reason, I am not convinced that the same political formula will produce identical results in Maharashtra.

Even if much of Bollywood or other influential voices oppose the BJP, Maharashtra's politics has traditionally been shaped more by local political realities than celebrity endorsements.

Whether this momentum becomes a lasting political movement or remains a temporary surge of public anger is something only time will answer.

Vikrant Meena Hemant Joshi.

CJP’s protest exposed something nobody is discussing.
The money.
I asked one simple question.
Who paid for all this?

A few months ago,
Abhijeet Dipke was in the US.

Then came a remark from the Chief Justice.
Then came a meme page.
Then came millions of views.

Then came coordinated amplification.
Bots.
Anonymous pages.
Influencers.

Reels appearing everywhere.

Suddenly, Dipke returned to India.
Permission was secured.

A protest site appeared at Jantar Mantar.
Tents went up.
Stages were built.
Food began arriving.

Then Sonam Wangchuk joined.
Celebrities appeared.
Political leaders followed.
Student wings mobilised.

The crowd grew.
The story changed.

What began as a NEET protest became a political spectacle.

So I stopped watching the videos.
I started calculating the bills.

The protest ran from 6 June to 20 July.
That is 45 days.

45 days of continuous operations.
Let us calculate the economic value.

Food and beverages: ₹13 crore.
Daily transportation: ₹3 crore.
Final-day mobilisation: ₹3 crore.
Stage, tents, sound: ₹2.5 crore.
Water and drinks: ₹2 crore.
Volunteer logistics: ₹1.5 crore.
Accommodation and boarding: ₹3 crore.
Senior legal services: ₹1.5 Crore.
Medical counters and emergency: ₹3 crore.
Banners and printing: ₹2 crore.
PR and digital production: ₹2.5 Crore.
Social-media operations: ₹3.5 crore.
Speakers and invited guests: ₹2.5 crore.
Administration and operations: ₹1.5 crore.
Technical support: ₹0.5 crore.
Contingency: ₹3 crore.
Special Fees: ₹5 Crore.

Subtotal: ~₹52 crore.

Then came 20 July.
Approx 50,000 people turned up.
As per Media.

50,000 people do not materialise from thin air.

They must be contacted.
Transported.
Directed.
Supplied with water.
Managed on the ground.

Another ₹5 crore.

Add the YouTube machinery.
Video teams.
Editors.
Content creators.
Social-media pages.
Real-time amplification.

Another ₹5 crore.

Add the wider digital amplification surrounding the final mobilisation: Another ₹5 crore.

Then came reports and visuals of celebrations and hospitality. Add: ₹1 crore.

The total Cost: ~₹68 crore.

Read that again.
₹68 crore.

This was not a few angry students carrying handmade placards.
This was an operation.

Money leaves fingerprints.
Logistics leave patterns.
Amplification leaves digital trails.

So who funded it?

If I answer that today,
my account may not survive tomorrow.

But one thing is difficult to ignore.
This was not spontaneous.

It was organised.
Resourced.
Planned.

The scale demands questions.
The logistics demand answers.
Someone financed this machinery.

This story is only beginning.

The funding trail is where I am headed next.

Recent assurances by JPNadda & DrJitendraSingh on withdrawing FIRs against peaceful CJP protesters (tied to education issues/NEET) are fresh from July 25 talks, with written guarantees & timelines promised.

I found no prominent, well-documented cases where *these specific leaders* failed to follow through on identical past assurances about dropping protest cases. 

Broader pattern in Indian politics (across parties/govts): 
- Assurances during farmers’ protests, CAA agitations, student movements etc. often led to partial/delayed withdrawals. 
- Reasons: federal structure (state police handle most FIRs), legal processes, probes into alleged violence, or shifting priorities. 
- BJP-ruled states sometimes acted faster on aligned protests; opposition states slower. 

Implementation here starts with FIR copies in days & full withdrawal “shortly.” Public scrutiny on follow-through is fair—politics rewards delivery over promises.

The post mocks Abhijeet Dipke (founder of satirical "Cockroach Janta Party"/CJP youth movement) protesting at Jantar Mantar over exam leaks (esp. NEET). It claims even after Dharmendra Pradhan resigned July 25 due to the pressure, Dipke kept protesting until a police warning on action vs rioters/antisocial elements (passport cancellation for violent ones reported; Tihar/NSA detention powers routine) made him "beg on knees: leave me alone!"

The video shows Dipke on knees amid chaos/crowd/police — actually from him emotionally celebrating the resignation win by dropping to knees & pounding the stage (or earlier plea for protest tents). The post twists it negatively.

**Mostly true on basics** (protests real, resignation happened, police warnings on violence existed). The "cockroach leader begging in fear" framing + exact 12-month Tihar order is exaggerated/misleading spin. Protests largely wound down after resignation; Dipke spoke of next steps. Satirical & derogatory tone.

VIDEO | Delhi: Reacting to the Delhi government's order stating that no adverse legal action will be taken against CJP protesters, Delhi Minister Ashish Sood says, "There had been an ongoing discussion regarding the premise that the Centre had made a promise to the protesting students who wanted to discuss their demands. The promise was that no lawsuits or punitive actions would be taken against students who participated in the protest. As the Supreme Court also observed, this undertaking does not apply to individuals who had prior criminal cases or were involved in violence and criminal activities. Action will continue to be taken against such individuals. The Supreme Court echoed this sentiment as well, and the Centre has fulfilled the promise it had made."

Earlier in the day, the Delhi government announced that it would refrain from taking any further adverse legal action against individuals involved in protests over alleged irregularities in the NEET (UG) examination. body:
Taking note of a plea on the use of metallic pellet guns during the recent students' protests against the NEET paper leak in Delhi, Supreme Court on Thursday asked Centre to preserve ammunition log of RAF deployed at Jantar Mantar.

Observing that police, as per  Bureau of Police Research and Development (BPRD) advisory, are empowered to use pellet guns in exceptional situations, top court termed “vague” the prayer in the plea seeking a complete ban on such usage.

A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana took note of submissions of senior advocate Vrinda Grover.

Former Central Information Commissioner and retired IPS officer Yashovardhan Azad and the two victims had moved court seeking a complete ban on use of metallic pellet guns to deal with law and order situations.

At theoutset, Justice Bagchi said that the prayer for a ban on the use of pellet guns by law enforcement agencies for civilian crowd dispersal was "vague" without challenging the police regulations, which permit the use of such weapons.

Grover said it was not easy to find such regulations in the public domain, and urged the bench to direct the Centre to place them on record.

Singh and Mansoori reportedly suffered pellet injuries during the ‘Sansad Chalo’ march called by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) on July 20.

Grover said as regards the petitioners, metallic pellets were used, and they were recovered from their bodies.

“I am not saying pellet guns should not be in the armoury of the RAF or not. Here it is different. They have used metallic pellets,” she said.

The bench said it was not averse to examining the use of pellets in a particular incident and the petitioners must show if it was permissible under a "graded approach".

The senior lawyer said she was confining her reliefs to metallic pellets.

"There is no standing order of the Delhi Police which permits the use of pellets. That is why my difficulty arises, and I have to rely on BPRD. If there is such a standing order, the Union may place it on record. I am sure the Union and the Delhi Police do not wish to fire pellets on innocent youngsters,” she said.

“I could not find any such standing order of the Delhi Police at all," Grover said.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said the government will do whatever is necessary to assist the bench.

Grover said the top court on July 28 directed the preservation of CCTV, drone, body camera footage and wireless logs and did not specifically refer to ammunition logs of the RAF.

“Whatever is required for investigation will be preserved,” solicitor general said.

The bench said a bona fide protest may turn violent at any point, perhaps due to the infiltration of anti-social elements, and “graded responses” by law enforcement might sometimes be necessary.

The forces may have to take on the spot decision based on the event, the law officer said.

Yashovardhan Azad approached the top court seeking a nationwide ban on the use of wholly or partly metallic pellet ammunition fired from pump-action or projectile action guns for dispersing civilian assemblies, contending that such weapons are inherently incompatible with constitutional standards governing the use of force.

The petition also sought exemplary compensation, comprehensive medical treatment and rehabilitation for all persons allegedly injured in the incident.

According to petition, RAF, deployed to assist Delhi Police in crowd management during protests, resorted to tear gas, lathi-charge and subsequently fired pump-action guns loaded with metallic pellets near Connaught Place.

The petitioners alleged that no prior warning or announcement was issued before the escalation in use of force and that several protesters suffered serious injuries, including eye injuries.

The protest broke out at Sarvodaya Inter College in Kishanpur area of Fatehpur(UP), where scores of students assembled on the campus and raised slogans against the school administration. Videos of the demonstration quickly went viral on social media, prompting district education officials to rush to the school and hold talks with the agitating students.  The students maintained that the protest was triggered by poor infrastructure and the absence of basic amenities.

According to officials, written assurances were given that four fans would be installed in every classroom within 24 hours, faulty electrical wiring would be repaired, an RO water cooler would be installed and desks and benches would be provided within a month. The students subsequently withdrew their protest after receiving the assurances.

body:
Supreme Court's interim order in the NEET protest cases draws a clear distinction between peaceful student protesters and individuals with prior criminal antecedents.

A Bench comprising the Chief Justice of India, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V. Mohana directed that investigations into the registered FIRs may continue, but no coercive action shall be taken against protesting students.

At the same time, the Court categorically clarified that this protection will NOT extend to persons with prior criminal antecedents. It also ordered the release of eligible juveniles on simple bonds and directed authorities to preserve CCTV, drone, body-camera and PCR footage from the protest sites.

However, CJP spokesperson Sourav Das publicly objected to this specific condition. Speaking to ANI, he said:

"अगर सुप्रीम कोर्ट बोल रही है कि जिनके ऊपर FIRs हैं पहले से उनको मत छोड़िए, तो वह हमें मंजूर नहीं है..."

This statement raises serious public-interest questions:

• Why oppose the Supreme Court's explicit exclusion of persons with prior criminal antecedents from interim protection?

• If the Court has consciously differentiated between genuine student protesters and those with existing criminal records, should that distinction not be respected?

• Does objecting to this condition undermine the Court's attempt to balance civil liberties with public safety and the rule of law?

The Supreme Court has not barred investigations. It has merely protected eligible students from coercive action while ensuring that those with prior criminal antecedents do not automatically receive the same relief.

The matter is now listed for further hearing on 3 August 2026, when the Union of India, the Government of NCT of Delhi and other concerned States will file their responses.

The debate is no longer just about protests—it is about whether judicial safeguards distinguishing peaceful demonstrators from repeat offenders should be respected.

body:
Across the streets of New Delhi and industrial hubs throughout Northern India, a vibrant, irreverent, and deeply angry youth movement has erupted into open defiance against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s far-right Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government. What began as an online meme responding to judicial arrogance has transformed into tens of thousands of students, unemployed workers, and young professionals paralyzing the capital. Calling themselves the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), these youth have reclaimed an ruling-class insult to build a formidable political force.

Yet, as state repression intensifies and the movement captures global attention, critical questions emerge regarding its leadership, class orientation, and revolutionary potential.

The Spark: Exam Scandals, Judicial Contempt, and the Birth of a Movement
The immediate catalyst for the uprising lies in India's deeply corrupt, highly centralized examination apparatus. On May 3, over 2.3 to 2.5 million high school graduates competed in the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET)—a brutally competitive exam determining entrance into medical colleges across India. For working-class families, NEET represents virtually the only avenue to secure one of approximately 50,000 public medical seats offering affordable tuition, as private institutions charge exorbitant fees far beyond the reach of average workers.

When revelations surfaced that NEET question papers had been leaked and sold by politically connected coaching syndicates, the exam was abruptly cancelled. Years of grueling study, immense emotional stress, and life savings invested by impoverished parents were wiped out in an instant. Tragically, at least 12 young people took their own lives in despair. Opposition sources highlight that over 152 centralized exam leaks have occurred under Modi's regime since 2014 without a single high-profile conviction, exposing systemic rot and state-sanctioned corruption.

"On May 15, Chief Justice Surya Kant sneered from the Supreme Court bench, denouncing unemployed youth protesting exam failures as 'parasites' and 'cockroaches.' Instead of breaking their spirit, the slur ignited a firestorm."

Adding fuel to the fire, Supreme Court Chief Justice Surya Kant openly sneered from the bench on May 15, denouncing India's unemployed youth as "parasites" and "cockroaches." Communications strategist Abhijeet Dipke—a Boston University graduate and former strategist for the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP)—capitalized on the remark by creating a viral satire account on Instagram: the Cockroach Janata Party, parodying the ruling BJP. Within days, the account amassed over 22 million followers, eclipsing every major political party in India and evolving from online satire into a physical mass sit-in at New Delhi's Jantar Mantar.

State Repression and "Sansad Chalo"
The scale of the movement reached a climax on July 20 during the opening of Parliament's Monsoon Session. Tens of thousands of young demonstrators launched a "Sansad Chalo" (March to Parliament), directly defying government bans. In response, the Modi government transformed central Delhi into a militarized zone under what local leaders termed a "marshal raj." Delhi Police and heavily armed paramilitary units—including the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and Rapid Action Force (RAF)—unleashed ferocious brutality.

Police fired tear gas into peaceful crowds, conducted indiscriminate baton charges (lathi charges), and locked down metro stations to prevent protesters from gathering. Over 200 youth suffered severe injuries, including skull lacerations and broken bones, with a 21-year-old female protester admitted to the ICU. Furthermore, authorities invoked the draconian National Security Act (NSA) of 1980, granting police sweeping powers to detain individuals without trial for up to a year. Environmental activist Sonam Wangchuk engaged in a 26-day hunger strike in solidarity, ending it only as public outrage reached a boiling point.

Despite the violence, the movement's sheer momentum forced the government onto the defensive. In a rare political concession, the administration was pressured into agreeing to a full-fledged Parliamentary discussion via an Adjournment Motion—a procedure unused in the lower house for 25 years. Member of Parliament Dr. John Brittas (CPI-M, Kerala) reported directly from the streets that MPs were forced to physically intercept police vans to free detained students, noting that Modi’s authoritarian hubris had been deeply dented.

Cultural Defiance, "Godi Media," and Subverting the State Narrative
In an interview with Democracy Now!, renowned writer and activist Arundhati Roy highlighted the transformative cultural shift driven by the young protesters. Unlike traditional, rigid political demonstrations, the youth movement is characterized by exuberant joy, satirical humor, music, and street theater. Demonstrators mock police water cannons by asking officers to turn them on to cool off in the Delhi heat, effectively stripping the regime of its fear factor.

Crucially, the youth have completely dismantled the state's media apparatus. For years, corporate-owned news channels—derisively termed "godi media" (laptop/lapdog media)—have served as propaganda outlets for Modi's regime, dominated by oligarchs like Ambani and Adani. When corporate journalists attempt to report from protest sites, students jeer and drive them away.

Instead, young protesters utilize Instagram reels, TikTok, YouTube, and encrypted channels to broadcast raw footage directly to global audiences. By bypassing traditional media, they expose the stark reality behind Modi's carefully crafted international image, turning his speeches into viral objects of ridicule and uniting youth across religious and caste lines—Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, and Christian alike.

Reformism vs. Class Revolution
While the CJP movement has successfully rattled the state, a rigorous socialist analysis reveals structural limits in its current program. The root of this youth explosion is not merely corrupt exam administrators, but the fundamental crisis of Indian capitalism. Official labor statistics reveal India's youth unemployment is at a 45-year high. Over 10 million young workers enter the labor market annually, only to face gig-economy exploitation, underemployment, or absolute poverty. This precarity exists alongside staggering inequality: India's 229 billionaires hoard over $1 trillion in net worth while public education and social services face chronic underfunding.

Supreme Court Interim Orders in CJP Protest Case (July 28, 2026)Bench: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V. Mohana.The Court was hearing a batch of petitions alleging police excesses (and related violence) during student protests over NEET paper leaks and exam irregularities, including the July 20 Parliament march in Delhi and incidents in other states. 

Key Interim DirectionsPreserve evidence: All CCTV footage, drone recordings, body-camera footage, wireless communication logs, and PCR records related to the protests must be preserved. 

Protect digital data: Police authorities must preserve the personal information and digital data of student protesters and ensure it is not brought into the public domain for the time being. No personal data or details of the protesters shall be published. 

No coercive action: No coercive steps shall be taken against students who protested, provided they have no criminal antecedents. (Investigations into registered FIRs may continue, but without coercive measures against eligible students.) 

Release of detainees: All states are directed to release students/children below the age of 18 years who were arrested or detained during the protests and who have no criminal antecedents. Broader directions also cover release of protesting students without criminal antecedents. 

Other Directions and ObservationsNotices issued to the Union of India, NCT of Delhi, and the states of Assam, Bihar, West Bengal, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, and Kerala (Chief Secretaries directed to respond). 

Allegations of excesses (including use of force against students and injuries to police personnel, reported as over 200–250) prima facie warrant a fair, independent, and transparent probe. The Court indicated it may constitute a high-powered committee/SIT (possibly headed by a former judge) after receiving replies from the Centre and states. The probe would address concerns from both sides. 

Evidence materials (including pen drives) were placed on record.
Next hearing: August 3, 2026.

These are interim measures reported from the hearing (primarily via LiveLaw updates and consistent coverage in other outlets). Full written order details may follow. The protection explicitly does not extend to persons with criminal antecedents.

🚨 Supreme Court Issues Interim Directions on Student Protest Cases

On 28 July 2026, a Supreme Court bench comprising CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi, and Justice V. Mohana heard a batch of petitions concerning alleged police excesses and counter-allegations of injuries to police during the recent student protests over exam irregularities and paper leaks, including the Jantar Mantar demonstrations associated with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

⚖️ Key observations by the Court:
• Peaceful protest is a constitutional right and the demonstrations were initially intended to remain peaceful.
• Violence during protests may sometimes be caused by "uninvited guests" or infiltrators, and not necessarily by the original protesters.
• The Court also noted that petitions have been filed on behalf of injured police personnel, making it clear that allegations from both sides require impartial examination.
• The bench found a prima facie case for an independent and fair investigation into the allegations.

📌 Possible SIT
The Court indicated that it may constitute a Special Investigation Team (SIT) headed by a former Supreme Court judge and sought responses from:

- Union Government
- Delhi Government (NCT)
- Assam
- Bihar
- West Bengal
- Uttar Pradesh
- Madhya Pradesh
- Maharashtra
- Kerala

🗓️ Next hearing: 3 August 2026

✅ Interim Directions
• Release all students arrested or detained for participating in the protests if they have no criminal antecedents.
• No coercive action against such students during the pendency of the matter.
• Preserve all relevant evidence, including CCTV footage, drone recordings, body-worn camera footage, wireless communications, PCR logs, and other records.
• Preserve protesters' personal information and digital data, and ensure it is not made public for the time being.
• The Court also emphasized revisiting protocols on handling demonstrations, reaffirming the principle of graduated use of force and stressing that mere participation in a protest does not justify excessive force.

⚠️ Important Clarification
Some posts on social media are portraying this as blanket protection for all protesters. That is not what the Court said.

The protection applies to students with no criminal antecedents, while any allegations of criminal conduct will still be investigated through due process and evidence. The Court's emphasis was on protecting peaceful protest while ensuring accountability wherever criminal acts are established.

This matter arises from the student protests over exam irregularities and paper leaks, including the NEET controversy, which triggered nationwide demonstrations and significant political fallout.

Future Move of CJP  

Now CJP has secured one resignation. That result has changed the incentives for them for future action.   

They tested an emotional issue, created visible pressure, and extracted a concession. When a method works, it is usually repeated and refined.  

If you analyse the movement The most likely approach from here is for them to look for the next issue that can be mobilised quickly and keep the government reactive.  

Some of the possible targets are:   

1. Another student-related failure  This remains the highest-probability path. Any fresh controversy in competitive exams (JEE, CUET, state exams), scholarship delays, fee hikes, or admission counselling glitches can be framed the same way as NEET. The template already exists: emotional stakes, large affected group, easy moral framing.  

2. Nicobar Island project  This can be positioned as an environmental and tribal rights issue. Large infrastructure in a sensitive zone offers a long campaign runway and multiple angles for sustained protest.  

3. AI Data Centers  These can be attacked on land use, water consumption, energy demand, and weak local job creation. For a generation already anxious about employment, the claim that such projects serve corporations more than citizens has natural appeal.  

In each case the method stays consistent: choose an issue with moral clarity, mobilise fast, amplify through media, and raise demands beyond easy concessions.  The first probe worked. 

The next phase will test whether the same playbook can extract a higher political cost.

CJP is celebrating the resignation of the Education Minister as some great "victory."

But ask them one simple question—how does one man's resignation fix systemic exam leaks or create a foolproof system?

They have no answer.

Most of them don't even know about the Radhakrishnan Committee or its recommendations. Why? Because they never wanted real, long-term solutions. They only wanted a political scalp.

This entire protest was never about education reform. It was a carefully orchestrated, politically motivated agitation backed by AAP, certain extremists, and the usual left-liberal gang whose only real agenda is to abuse Modi day and night.

Vulgar language, open hate, and pure political opportunism dressed up as student anger.

Resignation is not the solution. Structural reform is. And these people were never interested in that.

Here's the accurate data on the number of medical colleges and MBBS seats in India:

In 2014: • 387 medical colleges • 51,348 MBBS seats

In 2026: • 844 medical colleges • 1,39,489 MBBS seats

The number of medical colleges has more than doubled.

MBBS seats have nearly tripled.

This is real capacity building—not just slogans or protests demanding resignations.

While some are busy shouting for political optics, the actual expansion of medical education has been historic.

While you are criticising the government for not doing anything, you should first look at the numbers above.

Now let's come to the main argument.

According to me, the Education Minister should resign not because the NEET paper leak happened, as he had no direct role in it. It was carried out by paper setters and the coaching mafia.

However, he should resign for not implementing the Radhakrishnan Committee's recommendations in full.

The Radhakrishnan Committee's 101 recommendations are more than an anti-paper leak roadmap—they're a blueprint to rebuild trust in India's examination system.

Key reforms include:

🔹 Encrypted digital question paper delivery, printed only minutes before the exam.

🔹 Aadhaar + biometric + AI-based multi-stage candidate verification to curb impersonation.

🔹 AI-driven detection of cheating, suspicious score patterns, and malpractice.

🔹 Around 1,000 secure government testing centres with CCTV, mobile jammers, and standardised infrastructure.

🔹 Gradual shift to Computer-Based and Adaptive Testing.

🔹 Stronger cybersecurity, reduced outsourcing, dedicated vigilance and research wings, better grievance redressal, and mental health support.

The committee correctly identified that paper leaks aren't isolated failures—they're symptoms of systemic weaknesses across the entire exam lifecycle.

The solution, therefore, isn't just harsher punishment; it's structural reform through technology, governance, and accountability.

If implemented effectively, these reforms could significantly reduce paper leaks, improve transparency, restore public confidence, and modernise the examination process for the 2+ crore students who appear for competitive exams every year.

Now the real challenge is ensuring these recommendations move from paper to practice.

OF THE COCKROACH, THE SWEET (PEREMENDE) AND THE HYENA

Never underestimate the power of an insult. Sometimes the people you intend to demean take the insult, wear it as a badge of honour, and turn it against you.

Three stories — two from Kenya and one from India — illustrate this rather well: the cockroach, the peremende and the hyena.

THE COCKROACH — INDIA

India’s Education Minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, resigned on 25 July 2026 after weeks of protests over alleged examination irregularities, particularly the leakage of the NEET-UG examination used for admission to medical and other health-professional courses.

But one of the fascinating aspects of the protests is their name: the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

The story appears to have begun in May 2026 following remarks by a Supreme Court judge that were widely interpreted online as comparing unemployed or protesting young people to “cockroaches”. The Court subsequently clarified that the remarks had been taken out of context.

But by then, the cockroach had escaped.

Instead of running away from the derogatory label, young Indians appropriated it.

A satirical idea emerged online: if they were cockroaches, then perhaps they needed a Cockroach Janta Party.

The satire rapidly developed into a youth movement. When the NEET-UG examination controversy erupted, the CJP made it one of its major causes, demanding accountability and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

What began partly as internet satire became demonstrations, sit-ins and other forms of protest.

And eventually, the Minister resigned.

The cockroach had bitten back.

THE SWEET (PEREMENDE) — KENYA

We have seen something remarkably similar before in Kenya.

In 2012, Kenyan doctors were engaged in industrial action over their terms and conditions of service.

During the dispute, then Medical Services Minister Prof Peter Anyang’ Nyong’o was reported to have characterised the doctors as sulking children crying for peremende — sweets.

It was intended as a dismissive description. The doctors did something clever.They took the insult and owned it.

And so was born the #PeremendeMovement.

Doctors went online explaining exactly which “sweets” they wanted: adequate staffing, equipment, medicines, better working conditions and implementation of agreements reached with government.

Social media became an important part of the industrial action.

Instead of weakening the doctors, the peremende label gave their campaign an identity.

The strike eventually ended with a return-to-work agreement under which the government agreed to honour commitments previously made to doctors.

The sweet had become bitter for those who had coined the description.

THE HYENA (HITI) — KENYA, 2026

Fast-forward to July 2026.

Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale has found himself at the centre of controversy following remarks made partly in Somali during a public event in Lafey, Mandera.

At the heart of the dispute is a Somali proverb involving the waraabe — the hyena.

Duale has argued that he was using a traditional Somali proverb about the difficulty of abandoning an entrenched habit. His critics, however, interpreted his wider remarks as referring derogatorily to the Kikuyu community.

The reaction has been swift.

The National Cohesion and Integration Commission has opened investigations into complaints concerning the remarks. Political leaders have demanded an apology.

But something else is happening.

Some Kikuyus on social media have begun appropriating the hyena.

Instead of rejecting the label, they are making jokes about it, producing memes and videos and turning the animal into a symbol of resilience, organisation and collective strength.

The intended insult — or perceived insult — is acquiring a completely different meaning in the hands of those to whom it was allegedly directed.

It sounds strangely familiar.

Cockroach.

Peremende.

Hyena.

Different countries. Different circumstances. Different generations.

But there is a common lesson.

BE CAREFUL WHAT YOU CALL PEOPLE

History is full of examples of derogatory labels being appropriated by the very people they were intended to diminish.

Once that happens, the person who coined the insult loses control of its meaning.

An insult can give a previously scattered group a common identity.
- A joke can become a hashtag.
- A hashtag can become a movement.
- A movement can become political organisation.
- And political organisation can have consequences.

In India, what started as the satirical Cockroach Janta Party became part of a protest movement powerful enough to place enormous pressure on the government and culminate in the resignation of an Education Minister.

In Kenya in 2012, doctors transformed peremende from a dismissive description into the identity of a highly visible campaign during their industrial action.

And now, in 2026, we are watching the word fisi acquire a new political meaning almost in real time.

Whether the current fisi phenomenon disappears as another social-media joke or develops into something politically significant remains to be seen.

But politicians would do well to remember one thing:
- Never give an aggrieved population a name around which it can organise.
- You may intend it as an insult.
- They may turn it into their identity.
- And sometimes, that identity becomes a movement.

Time will tell what becomes of the hyena.

By framing legitimate law enforcement actions as persecution, this effort risks eroding public trust in our judiciary and police forces.

India deserves legal professionals who defend the Constitution impartially, not those who consistently align with narratives that weaken the nation’s resolve against internal disruptions.

Organised, premeditated, and far from any spontaneous citizen gathering. Meloni herself called it out as organised violence.

In Delhi, the numbers are almost identical: 118+ police personnel hurt, including senior officers (Special CP, Joint CP, ACPs), during clashes with CJP demonstrators.

Two police buses attacked, shops on Janpath vandalised, stone-pelting, property damage. Police have flagged anti-social elements with criminal records mixing into the crowds via facial recognition. This is definiteluly not a pure “student protest.”

NEET was already reconducted with stricter measures after the paper-leak mess. Stringent action was taken. Yet it was kept alive as a ready-made weapon, exactly the kind of grievance that gets amplified, prolonged, and then turned into street confrontation when the timing suits. We all saw the attacks on police. Uniforms do not make the injuries any less real.

Notice the pattern: simultaneous pressure on the forces that maintain order in two countries whose leaders (Modi and Meloni) have built unusually close personal and strategic ties, Indo-Mediterranean partnership, defence-tech cooperation, open alignment against the usual globalist currents. 

When leaders who refuse the script get stronger, the forces of disruption target the thin blue line that stands between chaos and governance.

This DS has inserted the professional riot cadre, attack the police, flood the narrative with “peaceful students/protesters,” and force governments onto the defensive. Italy’s black-bloc style assault and Delhi’s stone-and-vandalism phase are not coincidence. They are the same method applied on two fronts.

The public should see the method for what it is.

18-year-old NEET aspirant Sharim allegedly died by suicide on 13 June following the alleged NEET-UG paper leak controversy. A resident of Amarpur village in Uttar Pradesh's Bulandshahr district, Sharim had been preparing for NEET at Aakash Institute in Jasola, Delhi.

His elder brother, Firoz Qureshi, says he has been seeking justice ever since. According to Firoz, he first approached the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), requesting that Sharim's photograph and details be displayed on the protest stage, but alleges that his request was ignored.

Firoz further claims that on 15 June, he went to Shaheen Bagh Police Station to file a complaint, but alleges that the police did not take his concerns seriously.

According to Firoz, he made one final attempt on the last morning of the Jantar Mantar protest to raise his brother's case with CJP representatives, but says he was once again ignored.
